row.profile_notes:
According to the UK-Solicitors Regulation Authority: On November 02, 2016, Roland David Taylor received a written rebuke and was ordered to pay a financial penalty of GBP 1,500. He was also ordered to pay the SRA's costs of GBP 1,350 in investigation. Taylor trades as a recognised sole practice in the name of Roland Taylor & Co Solicitors whose office is at 21 West Drive, Wethersfield, Braintree, Essex, CM7 4BT. Mr Taylor was found to have failed to comply with an order made by the Legal Ombudsman and failed to keep the affairs of a client confidential. He thereby acted in breach of principles 6 and 7 of the SRA Principles 2011 and failed to achieve Outcome 4.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct 2011.

According to the UK-Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal; July 10, 2017: The Adjudicator found two allegations proved, namely that the Appellant Roland David Taylor : Allegation 1: Failed to comply with a decision of the Legal Ombudsman ("LeO") dated July 08, 2015, which directed that Mr Taylor should return the sum of GBP 6,085.93 to Mrs A, by the required dated of August 04, 2015 and was thereby in breach of Principles 6 and 7 of the SRA Principles 2011 ("the Principles"); Allegation 2: Released confidential information about his client (Mrs A) and thereby breached Principles 6 and 7 and failed to achieve Outcome 4.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct 2011 ("the Code"). The Adjudicator decided to: (a) Rebuke Mr Taylor, and to order the publication of this decision; (b) Direct that Mr Taylor pay a financial penalty and to order the publication of this; and (c) Direct that Mr Taylor pay the sum of GBP 1,350 in relation to the SRA's costs of investigating this matter.

Section-11EE prescribes restrictions on movements, residence & visits of these suspects. Section 11EE also states that suspects before leaving the area of residence have to seek prior permission of Officer In charge of Police Station. Their assets & sources of incomes will also be subject to investigation. ATA-1997 further provides that any person who violates any direction or order shall be punishable with an imprisonment of up to 3 years or fine or both. However, these provisions of ATA 1997 are not enforced effectively or uniformly. It is very rare to observe registration of cases against suspects u/s 11EE ATA 1997. row.details: enforcement: Debarred/Disciplined | US –Financial Industry Regulatory Authority | United States
row.profile_notes: According to United States-Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; June 2016: On April 08, 2016, Michael David Taylor was assessed a deferred fine of USD 5,000 and suspended from association with any FINRA member in any capacity for three months. Without admitting or denying the findings, Taylor consented to the sanctions and to the entry of findings that he circumvented his member firm’s annuity replacement procedures by failing to identify and submit variable annuity purchases totaling approximately USD 700,000 as annuity replacements, even though each purchase was funded by the sale of another annuity. The findings stated that Taylor concealed the replacement transactions from the firm’s supervisory review by transferring the proceeds from the replaced annuity to a firm money market account in the customer’s name. After waiting approximately 30 to 60 days, Taylor then used the funds in the money market account to purchase the new variable annuity. Taylor further concealed that the annuity purchases were replacements by providing inaccurate information on the transaction documents he submitted to the firm and the annuity companies. Taylor earned approximately USD 18,000 in additional commissions by submitting the annuity purchases as new trades rather than as annuity replacements. hits.first_para: According to United States-Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; June 2016: On April 08, 2016, Michael David Taylor was assessed a deferred fine of USD 5,000 and suspended from association with any FINRA member in any capacity for three months. Without admitting or denying the findings, Taylor consented to the sanctions and to the entry of findings that he circumvented his member firm’s annuity replacement procedures by failing to identify and submit variable annuity purchases totaling approximately USD 700,000 as annuity replacements, even though each purchase was funded by the sale of another annuity. The findings stated that Taylor concealed the replacement transactions from the firm’s supervisory review by transferring the proceeds from the replaced annuity to a firm money market account in the customer’s name. After waiting approximately 30 to 60 days, Taylor then used the funds in the money market account to purchase the new variable annuity. Taylor further concealed that the annuity purchases were replacements by providing inaccurate information on the transaction documents he submitted to the firm and the annuity companies. Taylor earned approximately USD 18,000 in additional commissions by submitting the annuity purchases as new trades rather than as annuity replacements. Taylor subsequently repaid these commissions to the firm. The suspension is in effect from April 18, 2016 to July 17, 2016.

row.profile_notes:
According to Ministerio Público, Fiscalía de la Nación del Perú; February 11, 2026: The Provincial Prosecutor's Office Specializing in Corruption Crimes by Officials in Lambayeque obtained an 18-year prison sentence for the former mayor of the Provincial Municipality of San Ignacio, Carlos Martínez, for the crime of embezzlement. He was also fined 620 days and disqualified from holding public office for 10 years. Along with him, other officials were also convicted of the same crime. Among them were the former manager of Territorial Planning and Urban Infrastructure, Álvaro Cabrera; the former head of Settlements, José Larraín; the former head of Logistics, Wilfredo Rivera; the former head of Treasury, Roel Aldana; and the former assistant to the Works Settlement office, William Díaz, who received sentences of up to 18 years in prison and were disqualified from holding public office. Likewise, José Larraín, Juan Reyes, and Luis Ancajima were convicted as accomplices to the crime of aggravated conspiracy, as they were members of the criminal organization "Los topos de San Ignacio". Manuel Ilatoma Gálvez was also convicted in this case, receiving a sentence of four years and 25 days in prison and a three-year disqualification from public office. José Zeña, Juan Ramos, Juan Nanfuñay, and Daniel Pisfil were also convicted. According to the report, they all embezzled PEN 762,000 in public funds by simulating contracts for alleged services involving the preparation of layout plans and topographic surveys.


De acuerdo con Ministerio Público, Fiscalía de la Nación del Perú; Febrero 11, 2026: La Fiscalía Provincial Especializada en Delitos de Corrupción de Funcionarios de Lambayeque logró una condena de 18 años de prisión para el exalcalde de la Municipalidad Provincial de San Ignacio, Carlos Martínez, por el delito de peculado doloso por apropiación. Asimismo, se le impuso una multa de 620 días multa y una inhabilitación para el ejercicio de la función pública por 10 años. Junto a él, también se obtuvo la sentencia de otros funcionarios por el mismo delito. Entre ellos el exgerente de Acondicionamiento Territorial e Infraestructura Urbana, Álvaro Cabrera; el exjefe de Liquidaciones, José Larraín; el exjefe de Logística, Wilfredo Rivera; el exjefe de Tesorería, Roel Aldana; y el exasistente de la oficina de Liquidación de Obras, William Díaz, quienes recibieron penas de hasta 18 años de prisión y fueron inhabilitados para ejercer la función pública. Asimismo, José Larraín, Juan Reyes y Luis Ancajima fueron sentenciados como cómplices del delito de asociación ilícita en su forma agravada, ya que fueron miembros de la organización criminal "Los topos de San Ignacio". Por este caso, también fue condenado Manuel Ilatoma Gálvez, quien recibió una sentencia de cuatro años y 25 días de prisión y una inhabilitación por tres años. También fueron condenados José Zeña, Juan Ramos, Juan Nanfuñay, Daniel Pisfil. De acuerdo con el informe, todos ellos se apropiaron de PEN 762 000 de fondos públicos, mediante la simulación de contratos por presuntos servicios de elaboración de planos de replanteo y levantamiento topográfico.

According to Contraloría General de la República de Perú; May 26, 2026: According to report Nº 021-2026-2-0222-SCE of May 14, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller General of the Republic of Peru identified alleged functional administrative responsibility in relation to officials of the National University of Trujillo (UNT): Hermes Natividad Sifuentes Inostroza (penal), Alberto Luis Cava Carhuayo (penal), Elmo Linder Cruzado Oliva (penal), Aleida Yamali González Acosta (penal), Luis Alberto Blas Baltodano (penal), Marilyn Solís Guzmán (penal), Anthony Frank Pérez Rosas, Milton Ricardo Gómez Silva (penal), Wilbbert Valdemar Vigo Alfaro (penal), Vicente Rusber Rodríguez Pérez, Pablo Aguilar Marin (penal), Victor Eduardo Lau Torres (penal), Soledad Janett Mostacero Llerena (penal), Víctor Javier Vásquez Villalobos (penal), Teódulo Jenaro Santos Cruz (penal), Orlando Velásquez Benites (penal), José Erli Tantaleán Vásquez (penal), Francisco Manuel Escalante Correa (penal), and Evelyn Mollo Villanueva (penal). This is due to the fact that the appointment and acceptance into positions subject to free appointment and removal of public servants who did not demonstrate compliance with the requirements established in the Position Classification Manual, Law n° 31419, and its Regulations, resulted in the proper functioning of the public administration being affected, as well as the suitability and legality of access to and the exercise of public office.


De acuerdo con Contraloría General de la República de Perú; Mayo 26, 2026: Según el informe N° 021-2026-2-0222-SCE de Mayo 14, 2026, la Contraloría General de la República de Perú identificó presunta responsabilidad administrativa funcional en relación a funcionarios de la Universidad Nacional de Trujillo (UNT): Hermes Natividad Sifuentes Inostroza (penal), Alberto Luis Cava Carhuayo (penal), Elmo Linder Cruzado Oliva (penal), Aleida Yamali González Acosta (penal), Luis Alberto Blas Baltodano (penal), Marilyn Solís Guzmán (penal), Anthony Frank Pérez Rosas, Milton Ricardo Gómez Silva (penal), Wilbbert Valdemar Vigo Alfaro (penal), Vicente Rusber Rodríguez Pérez, Pablo Aguilar Marin (penal), Victor Eduardo Lau Torres (penal), Soledad Janett Mostacero Llerena (penal), Víctor Javier Vásquez Villalobos (penal), Teódulo Jenaro Santos Cruz (penal), Orlando Velásquez Benites (penal), José Erli Tantaleán Vásquez (penal), Francisco Manuel Escalante Correa (penal) y Evelyn Mollo Villanueva (penal). Esto debido a que la designación y aceptación en cargos de libre designación y remoción a servidores públicos que no acreditaron el cumplimiento de los requisitos establecidos en el Manual de Clasificador de cargos, Ley n° 31419 y su Reglamento, generó que se afecte el correcto funcionamiento de la administración pública; así como la idoneidad y legalidad en el acceso y ejercicio de la función pública.

row.position_or_allegation: Sentenced to seven years and six months for money laundering, fraud, forgery, and organized crime - July 18, 2007.
row.details: adverse_media: Forgery/Organized Crime/Fraud/Money Laundering | Incident
row.relationships: de Sousa Machado, Rosimar (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); Fernandes de Souza, Antônio Francisco (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); Monteiro Oliveira, Adalberto (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); da Silva, Fábio Florêncio (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); Evangelista de Araújo, Ataíde (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia)
row.profile_notes:
According to conjur.com.br; July 18, 2007: The Federal Justice of Pará sentenced Francisco Correa Nobre Neto to seven years and six months for money laundering, fraud, forgery, and organized crime as part of Operation “Cavalo de Tróia”, launched in November 2003 by the Federal Police. According to a complaint of the Federal Public Ministry, Nobre Neto was member of a criminal organization, active in Parauapebas (PA), that fraudulently access current accounts and third-party savings accounts through e-mails to show bank false pages or were invaded by spy programs that captured customer information. In this way, criminals were able to withdraw money and then conceal and disguise the source of funds by renting the checking account and other people's cards and the practice of registering property on behalf of third parties. The damage caused is difficult to measure accurately according to the responsibles of the financial institutions.


De acordo com conjur.com.br; Julho 18, 2007: A Justiça Federal do Pará condenou Francisco Correa Nobre Neto a sete anos e seis meses por lavagem de dinheiro, estelionato, fraude ideológica e crime organizado como parte da Operação “Cavalo de Tróia”, deflagrada em Novembro 2003 pela Polícia Federal. Segundo a denúncia do Ministério Público Federal, Nobre Neto era membro de uma quadrilha, atuante em Parauapebas (PA), para acessar de forma fraudulenta as contas-correntes e de poupança de terceiros, por meio de emails para mostrar paginas falsas dos bancos ou eram invadidos por programas espiões que capturavam as informações cadastrais dos clientes. De esse jeito os criminais conseguiam sacar dinheiro para logo ocultar e dissimular a origem dos recursos através do ‘aluguel’ da conta-corrente e de cartões alheios e da prática de registrar bens em nome de terceiras pessoas. O prejuízo causado e dificil de mesurar com precisão segundo responsaveis das institucões financeiras afetadas.

row.position_or_allegation: Fined for fraud and embezzlement - June 08, 2021.
row.details: enforcement: Embezzlement | BR - Ministério Público do Estado do Amazonas | Brazil; adverse_media: Fraud/Embezzlement | Incident
row.relationships: Mendonça, Marco Aurélio (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia,PEP); Pampulha Construções e Montagens Ltda (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); Conte Galate, Rosário (Associate; Enforcement); Bitar Ruas, Antunes (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia,Enforcement); Rayol Cavalcante Oliveira, Tyssia Régia (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); Fonseca, Faustiniano (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia,Enforcement); Fernandes Lages, Alexandre Magno (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia); Gomes de Oliveira, André (CoDefendant; AdverseMedia,Enforcement)
row.profile_notes:
According to tjam.jus.br; June 08, 2021: Francisco Corrêa de Lima was sentenced for fraud and embezzlement. According to investigations, in November, 2007, Corrêa de Lima was involved in fraud committed in an agreement intended for the execution of works to improve and expand the road system in five cities in the interior of Amazonas State. Through an inspection it was found that the works requested were not executed as reported, even when the state transferred BRL 17,246,010.10 out of the BRL 34,943,716.30 stated in the contract. Corrêa de Lima had his political rights suspended for five years, public function suspended, and was fined 10 times the amount received as profit at the time the facts took place.

According to BR - Ministério Público do Estado do Amazonas: September 03, 2019: On August 27, 2019, the Public Ministry of Amazonas accused Seinfra supervisor Francisco Corrêa de Lima and other individuals of administrative misconduct in the construction of a bridge in the Philadelphia Community, in the rural area of Santo Antônio do Iça. According to the complaint, the construction of the bridge began between June and August 2006 reaching BRL 1,600,000,000.00, however, on June 21, 2010, the State Court of Audits found that the bridge had collapsed.

According to consultasaj.tjam.jus.br; April 29, 2009: The Court of Justice received the complaint filed by the Public Ministry of Amazonas against Francisco Corrêa de Lima and others for fraud and embezzlement. According to the complaint, the group was involved in fraud committed in a contract valued at BRL 34,943,716.30.


De acordo com tjam.jus.br; Junho 08, 2021: Francisco Corrêa de Lima foi condenado por fraude e peculato. Segundo investigações, em Novembro de 2007, Corrêa de Lima esteve envolvido em fraude cometida em convênio destinado à execução de obras de melhoria e ampliação do sistema viário em cinco municípios do interior do Estado do Amazonas. Por meio de fiscalização, constatou-se que as obras solicitadas não foram executadas conforme informado, mesmo quando o estado repassou BRL 17.246.010,10 dos BRL 34.943.716,30 previstos em contrato. Corrêa de Lima teve seus direitos políticos suspensos por cinco anos, função pública suspensa e foi multado em 10 vezes o valor recebido a título de lucro na época dos fatos.

De acordo com BR - Ministério Público do Estado do Amazonas: Setembro 03, 2019: Em Agosto 27, 2019, o Ministério Público do Amazonas acusou o fiscal da Seinfra, Francisco Corrêa de Lima, e outros indivíduos de improbidade administrativa na construção da Ponte na Comunidade Filadélfia, na zona rural do Município. Segundo a denúncia, a construção da ponte começou entre junho e agosto de 2006 atingindo o valor de BRL 1.600.000.000,00, no entanto, no dia 21 de junho de 2010, o Tribunal de Contas do Estado verificou que a ponte entrou em colapso e desabou.

De acordo com consultasaj.tjam.jus.br; Abril 29, 2009: O Tribunal de Justiça recebeu denúncia do Ministério Público do Amazonas contra Francisco Corrêa de Lima e outros por fraude e peculato. De acordo com a denúncia, o grupo estava envolvido em fraude cometida em contrato no valor de BRL 34.943.716,30.

According to United States - Colorado Attorney General and the Department of Law, United States - Vermont Attorney General, United States - New York State Attorney General, United States - Massachusetts Attorney General, United States - Connecticut Attorney General, United States - Virginia Attorney General, United States - Tennessee Attorney General, United States - Texas Attorney General, United States - Delaware Attorney General and the Department of Justice, United States - California Attorney General, United States - Pennsylvania Attorney General, United States - Montana Attorney General and United States - Florida Attorney General; January 23, 2025: Published on that date, settlement reached USD 7,400,000,000 against Purdue Pharma for creating the opioid crisis. Purdue invented, manufactured, and aggressively marketed opioids for decades, fueling waves of addiction and overdose deaths across the country. The settlement ends the Sacklers’ control of Purdue and their ability to sell opioids in the United States. Purdue will continue to be overseen by a monitor and will be prevented from lobbying or marketing opioids under the settlement. A significant amount of the settlement funds will be distributed in the first three years, with the Sacklers paying USD 1,500,000,000 and Purdue paying nearly USD 900,000,000 in the first payment, followed by USD 500,000,000 after one year, an additional $500 million after two years, and USD 400,000 after three years.

Colorado will receive approximately USD 81,000,000 from the settlement;
Vermont will receive USD 22,000,000;
New York will receive USD 250,000,000 from the settlement; 
Massachusetts will receive USD 90,000,000;
Florida will receive between USD 233,370,000 - 325,930,000;
Connecticut will receive approximately USD 64,000,000 from the settlement; 
Virginia will receive approximately USD 107,400,000 from the settlement; 
Tennessee will receive more than USD 90,000,000; 
Delaware will receive over USD 27,000,000;
California expected to receive hundreds of millions of dollars;
Pennsylvania will receive up to USD 212,000,000 from the settlement;
Montana will receive nearly USD 4,000,000.

According to United States - Department of Justice; October 21, 2020: On October 21, 2020, Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty to three felony counts for defrauding the United States and violating the Anti-Kickback Statute from 2009 to 2017.  In addition to agreeing to plead guilty to these three felonies counts, the company has agreed to a USD 3,544,000,000, criminal fine and a USD 2,000,000,000 criminal forfeiture amount.  Further, to resolve its civil liability, Purdue Pharma has agreed to USD 2,800,000,000 in damages to the United States.  The company is in bankruptcy, so the corporate resolution is subject to the bankruptcy court’s approval.  If approved, this will be a corporate settlement totaling more than USD 8,300,000,000.  Additionally, members of the Sackler family have agreed to pay USD 225,000,000,000 in a civil settlement that will provide civil releases only.

According to theguardian.com; August 19, 2020: Published on that date, A Department of Justice internal memorandum obtained that Purdue Pharma have committed wire fraud and money laundering crimes to boost sales of its billion-dollar OxyContin opioid.

According to United States - California Attorney General; October 03, 2019: On October 03, 2019, an amended complaint lawsuit against filed against Purdue Pharma, adding eight additional members of the Sackler family. In the lawsuit, it is alleged that Purdue misleadingly introduced OxyContin into the market as a safe and effective treatment for chronic, non-cancer pain. As early as February 1997, Purdue and certain of the Sackler defendants knew that oxycodone-containing drugs like OxyContin were among the most abused opioids in the United States. Yet, between 1996 and 2002, Purdue more than doubled its sales force, and sales rose from approximately USD 48,000,000 to nearly USD 2,000,000,000  in 2002. These sales were made by representatives falsely promoting OxyContin as a drug that was neither addictive nor subject to withdrawal symptoms, while minimizing its potential for abuse and addiction. By March 2000, Purdue was aware of specific reports made to the company about the abuse and diversion of OxyContin occurring in communities across the United States. In fact, in 2007, Purdue and a number of its executives pleaded guilty to felony misbranding of OxyContin, admitting that they illegally promoted OxyContin. Purdue agreed to pay over USD 600,000,000 in criminal and civil penalties, fines, and forfeitures.

Purdue continued its deceptive marketing and promoting of OxyContin. Their revenues amounted to USD 3,000,000,000  in 2010, and as much as USD 1,800,000,000 as recently as 2017. The lawsuit further alleges that as part of its aggressive deceptive marketing campaign, Purdue distributed literature and other materials that misrepresented the safety of its opioid products to healthcare professionals and patients in California and elsewhere. Purdue sales representatives further pushed physicians to prescribe opioids to “trusted” patients, and implied that healthcare professionals could screen out potential addicts through urine tests and patient contracts. In addition to the amended complaint, Attorney General also joined a coalition of 23 attorneys general and formally opposed Purdue Pharma’s request to make USD 38,000,000 in bonus, incentive, and other payments to employees.

According to the United States - Rhode Island Attorney General, United States - Virginia Attorney General and United States - Pennsylvania Attorney General; September 11, 2019: On September 11, 2019, The State of Rhode Island, by and through its Attorney General, brings this action pursuant to his statutory and common law authority to redress Richard S. Sacker's, Jonathan D. Sackler's, Mortimer D.A. Sackler's, Kathe A. Sackler's, Ilene Sackler Lefcourt's, David A. Sackler's, and Beverly Sackler's (together, the Sacklers) campaign to unlawfully promote and distribute opioids in Rhode Island through their control and use of Purdue Pharma, L.P.'s, Purdue Pharma Inc.'s, the Purdue Frederick Company ( together, Purdue), and the fraudulent transfer of funds generated from such sales to the Sacklers and Prescription opioid are dangerous drugs that have harmed the public health, safety and welfare affecting every community in our State causing the epidemic of opioid addiction and death.

Rhode Island government committed to continuing to aggressively pursue our claims against Purdue Pharma and the Sacklers. On September 11, 2019, filed a complaint against additional members of the Sackler family for the role that they played in the distribution of these highly addictive opioids in Rhode Island.

According to United States - Rhode Island Attorney General; August 16, 2019: Published on that date, The Lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma Inc. for pharma trafficking. The lawsuit alleges that defendant opioid manufacturers and distributors knowingly misrepresented the risk posed by prescription opioids in order expand their use and drive-up profits. It is also alleged that, in particular, opioid distributors disregarded obligations to identify suspicious orders and customers, allowing for and failing to stop the diversion of opioids within and to Rhode Island.

According to United States - Arizona Attorney General; July 31, 2019: On July 31, 2019, Lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma Inc. And others for engaging in deceptive and misleading marketing to push opioids in violation of a 2007 judgment obtained by the Arizona Attorney General’s Office for violating the state’s Consumer Fraud Act.

The defendants allegedly disregarded the judgment and continued to disseminate false, misleading, or unbalanced information through Purdue’s sales representatives, advertising materials, and websites. The State also alleges that they violated the judgment by improperly marketing prescription opioids, including OxyContin, through seemingly independent nonprofits that were paid millions of dollars by Purdue to promote prescription opioids.

According to United States - Nevada Attorney General; June 17, 2019: On June 17, 2019, lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma Inc. and others for violations of the Nevada Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit alleges that the manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies, and individuals created an ecosystem of addiction with deadly consequences to the state and its residents for their own profit. Through a systematic marketing campaign, sham “medical” organizations, funded experts, and other shameful tactics, the defendant’s peddled false science designed to demonstrate that opioids were a safe, non-addictive treatment for pain. The defendants furthered their wrongful conduct by encouraging doctors to treat addiction with more opioids and intensify the epidemic they created. Even when opioid deaths skyrocketed, the defendants simply redesigned their marketing campaign to continue to reap profits at the expense of Nevadans. Legal causes of action include violations of Nevada’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, False Claims Act, Racketeering Act, negligence, and public nuisance.

The Complaint lists over 40 defendants. Manufacturer defendants include Purdue Pharma Inc. Manufacturer Defendants have packaged, distributed, supplied, sold, placed into the stream of commerce, labeled, described, marketed, advertised, promoted and purported to warn or purported to inform prescribers and users regarding the benefits and risks associated with the use of the prescription opioid drugs. 

According to United States - Hawaii Attorney General, United States - Maine Attorney General, United States - California Attorney General and United States - District of Columbia Attorney General; June 03, 2019: Published on that date, Purdue Pharma L.P., Purdue Pharma Inc. (Purdue), certain of its affiliates, and Dr. Richard S. Sackler was sued for unlawful practices in the marketing, sale, and distribution of opioids. The lawsuit alleges that Purdue’s illegal and misleading marketing and sales practices played a major role in contributing to the nationwide opioid crisis. It further alleges that Purdue created a public nuisance through its marketing and sale of opioids and misled healthcare professionals and patients about the addictive nature of opioids and their potential for abuse and diversion.

According to United States - Pennsylvania Attorney General, United States - Iowa Attorney General, United States - Maryland Attorney General, United States - Minnesota Attorney General, United States - Oregon Department of Justice Office of the Attorney General and United States - Kansas Attorney General; May 2019: In May 2019, a lawsuit was filed against Purdue Pharma, the creator of prescription painkiller OxyContin, accusing the company of a multi-faceted, illegal effort to market OxyContin in Pennsylvania. Shapiro’s suit is the first to specifically detail Purdue’s barrage of sales representatives targeting Pennsylvania doctors as a key facet of their campaign to push addictive opioids on Pennsylvanians.

The lawsuit alleges that Purdue launched an illegal marketing campaign of deception targeting Pennsylvania doctors and patients to change attitudes, practices, and the culture surrounding pain management. Some of the most egregious components of the campaign include Purdue deployed their highly trained sales staff to blanket Pennsylvania, making sales calls and in-person visits to physicians, totaling more than half a million visits in Pennsylvania alone, an amount second to only California. Purdue targeted Pennsylvania doctors with suspicious prescribing activity and would invest more sales force and marketing to get those doctors to prescribe even more OxyContin – sometimes resulting in as much as a 500% increase in OxyContin prescriptions by one office alone. Purdue misinformed doctors and pharmacists about the addictive nature of OxyContin and used industry thought leaders and in-house marketing literature to dispel the facts about the drug. As the opioid epidemic grew, Purdue created “pseudo-addiction,” a Purdue-conjured disease that showed similar equities as addiction but was to be treated, according to Purdue, with additional opioids. The Office of Attorney General is demanding that the Court issue an order preventing Purdue and anyone associated with Purdue’s misconduct from continuing to engage in these same deceptive tactics. 

According to United States - Illinois Attorney General; April 8, 2019: On April 8, 2019, Lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma L.P. and Purdue Pharma Inc. over its deceptive marketing practices designed to significantly increase prescriptions issued for opioids.

Between 2008 and 2017, Purdue dispatched sales representatives to Illinois hundreds of thousands of times. Raoul alleged Purdue also funded third-party publications under the guise of educational materials to promote opioids and downplay their risks, using terms like “pseudo addiction.” Sales representatives informed doctors and patients that the risks could be controlled. Despite knowing that its opioid painkillers were dangerous and being misused and diverted, Purdue allegedly targeted doctors with addicted patients and whose patients were diverting drugs for unlawful use. Raoul alleged that Purdue’s tactics tripled prescriptions of its opioids in Illinois.

According to United States - New York State Attorney General; March 28, 2019: Published on that date, The lawsuit filed Purdue Pharma Inc. against for engaging in healthcare fraud. 

Pursuant to Executive Law § 63(12), From manufacturing, distributing, selling, or marketing opioids within the State unless it complies with heightened, independently monitored safeguards against the recurrence of its fraudulent, illegal, and/or unlawful practices, which are to be set forth in a compliance plan reviewed and approved by Plaintiff and the Court.  Pursuant to Executive Law § 63(12), Pay restitution and damages for its fraudulent and/or illegal practices that violated that statute and caused compensable injuries to Plaintiff or any other person; and disgorge all profits it wrongfully obtained as a result of its fraudulent and/or illegal practices in violation of that statute.

According to United States - Utah Attorney General; January 30, 2019: Published on that date, The Utah Attorney General’s Office filed an administrative action against Purdue Pharma Inc. and others as part of the State’s efforts to hold accountable the opioid companies and individuals that created and fueled the opioid epidemic throughout Utah.

In the filing, under Utah Code, the Division of Consumer Protection of the Department of Commerce issued an administrative action, in the form of a citation, against the defendants alleging violations of the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act. An administrative proceeding allows the State to seek to prove its claims and obtain a judgment, injunctive relief, and civil penalties more promptly than state district court proceedings. Based on evidence that has emerged over 2018, this administrative action alleges that not only Purdue, but two of its owners also participated in Purdue’s fraudulent conduct.

According to United States - Connecticut Attorney General; December 20, 2018: Published on that date, the lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma Inc. and other affiliates for alleging that they designed, financed and waged a pervasive and aggressive campaign to mislead doctors and patients, claiming that prescription opioid medications manufactured and marketed by the company were safe and effective and strategically downplaying risks of addiction that they knew were inherent in their opioid products.

The state alleges that Purdue misinformed patients and doctors to get more and more people taking its premier opioid drug, OxyContin, and its two other opioid medications, Hysingla and Butrans. Purdue allegedly led patients and doctors to believe that opioids were safe to treat even minor pain, and that patients could and should take higher and more dangerous doses. The state alleges that Purdue sent sales representatives to doctors' offices, clinics, pharmacies and hospitals in Connecticut to make deceptive sales pitches about opioid drugs; rewarded high-prescribing doctors with attention, meals, gifts and money; and awarded prizes and bonuses to sales representatives who generated the most opioid prescriptions. In Connecticut, 1038 people died of accidental drug overdoses in 2017, the vast majority from opioid-related overdoses. The Connecticut Office of the Chief Medical Examiner has projected that 1030 more people will die of overdoses in 2018. From 2013 to 2016, Connecticut experienced a fourfold increase in deaths from prescription opioid overdoses, and the estimated economic cost of the opioid epidemic in Connecticut in 2016 was USD 10,270,000,000.

According to United States - Florida Attorney General-Sixth Judicial Circuit: November 16, 2018: Published on that date, an amended complaint was filed against opioid manufacturers and distributors including Purdue Pharma Inc. Allegedly, defendants deceptively, unfairly, and unconscionably sought to convince prescribers and patients that opioids are safe, rarely addictive, and necessary for treating a wide range of common ailments. Defendants spread these myths knowing that opioids create physical dependency within days or weeks; that withdrawal from prescription opioids can be agonizing; that long-term and high-dose opioid use is particularly likely to lead to addiction; and that high doses of opioids can be fatal. Defendants at all levels of the supply chain manufacturers, distributors, and chain pharmacies continued selling opioids in Florida even though they knew or should have known that the drugs were being diverted and misused for non-medical purposes. Defendants had duties to identify and stop suspicious orders and purchases, and to put in place reasonable policies to safeguard against diversion.

According to United States - Oregon Department of Justice Office of the Attorney General; September 13, 2018: Published on that date, the complaint alleges on Purdue Pharma Inc and Purdue deceptively marketed OxyContin to Oregon seniors, misrepresented the risks and benefits of the drug, and lied to the Oregon Board of Pharmacy, all to maximize Purdue’s profits. It states that over the last decade Purdue has engaged in a pattern of racketeering and misleading activity in Oregon.

he complaint, filed in Multnomah Circuit Court, details how Purdue’s conduct violated an agreed upon stipulated 2007 Oregon judgment resulting from an earlier investigation of its unlawful practices, as well as four distinct Oregon laws: The Unlawful Trade Practices Act, the Elderly Persons and Persons with Disabilities Abuse Prevention Act, the False Claims Act and the Oregon Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act.

According to United States - Rhode Island Attorney General and United States - Virginia Attorney General; June 2018: On June 25, 2018, A civil lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma Inc., for prescription opioid manufacturers and distributors over their alleged campaign of unfairly, deceptively, and fraudulently marketing and promoting opioids in Rhode Island.

According to the Complaint, distributors persistently disregarded their obligations to identify suspicious orders and customers, facilitating and failing to stop the diversion of opioids within and to Rhode Island. Rhode Island's Medicaid program spent more than USD 6,000,000 to pay for prescriptions of Purdue-branded opioids, along with additional funds for Purdue's generic opioids and for the costs of providing and using opioids long-term to treat chronic pain.

According to United States - Florida Attorney General, United States - North Carolina Attorney General, United States - North Dakota Attorney General and United States - Texas Attorney General; May 15, 2018: Published on that date, a lawsuit was filed against Purdue Pharma Inc., for allegedly using a campaign of misrepresentations and omissions about the use of opioids to doctors and consumers in order to increase prescriptions and opioid use, including false statements about the addictive nature of opioids and omissions of the severe risks posed by taking opioids. 

The opioid distributors allegedly shipped inordinately high volumes of opioids to customers in Florida and failed to report these suspicious orders of opioids, thereby fueling widespread diversion of opioids throughout the state. In the complaint filed the defendants’ actions violated the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, the Florida RICO Act, and violated common law public nuisance and negligence.

According to United States - South Dakota Attorney General; March 14, 2018: On March 14, 2018, Attorney General announced that his office has filed a civil lawsuit in South Dakota State Circuit Court against prescription drug manufactures Purdue, Endo and Janssen for deceptive marketing and sale of prescription opioids.

According to United States - Delaware Attorney General and the Department of Justice; January 19, 2018: On January 19, 2018, A lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma Inc for engaging in false, deceptive and unfair marketing of prescription opioids.

Purdue Pharma Inc engaged, and continue to engage, in a massive marketing campaign to misstate and conceal the risks of treating chronic pain with opioids. Although manufacturers are prohibited from marketing opioids through misstatements or omissions of material facts, Manufacturer Defendants nonetheless disseminated misstatements through multiple channels. This campaign includes websites, promotional materials, conferences, guidelines for doctors, and other vehicles.

Defendant Purdue Pharma Inc. is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of New York State with its principal place of business located in Stamford, Connecticut. During all relevant times, Purdue Pharma Inc. has manufactured and distributed substantial amounts of prescription opioids that have been and continue to be sold in Delaware. Purdue Pharma Inc. has engaged in consensual commercial dealings with Delaware and its citizens and has purposefully availed itself of the advantages of conducting business with and within Delaware.  

According to United States - Washington Attorney General: September 28, 2017: Published on that date, A lawsuit filed against OxyContin maker Purdue Pharma, Inc for fueling the opioid epidemic in Washington state, embarking on a massive deceptive marketing campaign and convincing doctors and the public that their drugs are effective for treating chronic pain and have a low risk of addiction, contrary to overwhelming evidence. This deceptive marketing resulted in the deaths of Washingtonians and devastation to Washington families. The City of Seattle filed a separate lawsuit against Purdue.

The lawsuit contends Purdue conducted an uncontrolled experiment on the American public without any reliable clinical evidence that opioids are effective at treating chronic pain. To doctors and patients, Purdue consistently downplayed the risks of addiction from long-term use and deceptively represented opioids as safe for treating long-term chronic pain.

According to United States - New Jersey Bureau of Securities; October 31, 2017: On October 31, 2017, A lawsuit filed against  Purdue Pharma L.P and its co defendants Purdue Pharma Inc. and Purdue Frederick Company alleging a direct link between New Jersey’s opioid crisis and a push by Purdue to boost profits by deceptively marketing addictive medications and exploiting vulnerable new markets, such as the elderly and the “opioid-naïve. The lawsuit charges Purdue with widespread deception about the risks and benefits of these dangerously addictive pain medications.

According to United States - New Mexico Attorney General: September 7, 2017: On September 7, 2017, Attorney General Hector Balderas announced that he has brought a lawsuit on behalf of the State of New Mexico against the country’s largest manufacturers and wholesale distributors of opioids, a crucial first step toward holding these companies responsible for flooding New Mexico’s communities with prescription opioids and fueling the opioid epidemic by putting profits over people. The State of New Mexico is filing suit against five of the largest manufacturers of prescription opioids and their related companies and against the country’s three largest wholesale drug distributors. The manufacturing companies pushed highly addictive, dangerous opioids, falsely representing to doctors that patients would only rarely succumb to drug addiction, while the distributors breached their legal duties to monitor, detect, investigate, refuse and report suspicious orders of prescription opioids.

Complaint against Defendants Purdue Pharma L.P., Purdue Pharma, Inc., The Purdue Frederick Company, Inc., Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, LTD., Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc., Cephalon, Inc., Johnson & Johnson, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Ortho-McNeil-Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. n/k/a Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Janssen Pharmaceutica Inc. n/k/a Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Endo Health Solutions Inc., Endo Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Allergan PLC f/k/a Actavis PLS, Watson Pharmaceuticals, Inc. n/k/a Actavis, Inc., Watson Laboratories, Inc., Actavis, LLC, Actavis Pharma, Inc. f/k/a Watson Pharma, Inc., McKesson Corporation, Cardinal Health, Inc., Cardinal Health 105, LLC, Cardinal Health 108, LLC, Cardinal Health 110, LLC, Cardinal Health 200, LLC, Cardinal Health 414, LLC, Cardinal Health Pharmacy Services, LLC, and AmerisourceBergen Drug Corporation and alleges, upon information and belief, as follows.

Opioid manufacturers, including Defendants Endo Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and Purdue Pharma L.P., have entered into settlement agreements with public entities that prohibit them from making many of the misrepresentations identified in this Complaint. Yet even afterward, each Manufacturer Defendant continued to misrepresent the risks and benefits of longterm opioid use in New Mexico and continues to fail to correct its past misrepresentations.

According to United States - Connecticut Attorney General, United States - Arizona Attorney General, United States - Idaho Attorney General, United States - District of Columbia Attorney General, United States - Vermont Attorney General, United States - Washington Attorney General, United States - Wisconsin Department of Justice - Office of the Attorney General, United States - Texas Attorney General, United States - Ohio Attorney General; May, 2007: Published on that date, Attorney General announced a USD 19,500,000 multi-state settlement with Purdue Pharma.  According to the complaint, which was filed with the settlement, Purdue initially marketed OxyContin principally for treatment of chronic pain in cancer patients. But that quickly changed. Starting in 1996, the company expanded its marketing program to focus on primary care physicians and encouraged OxyContin to treat a wider pool of patients and conditions.

According to United States Colorado Attorney General and the Department of Law, United States New York State Attorney General, United States Idaho Attorney General, United States Minnesota Attorney General, United States Iowa Attorney General, United States Pennsylvania Attorney General, United States Nevada Attorney General,  United States Virginia Attorney General, United States Hawaii Attorney General, United States Maine Attorney General; United States Wisconsin Department of Justice - Office of the Attorney General and United States Massachusetts Attorney General; July, 2021: On July 08, 2021, Resolution of the State’s lawsuit filed against the Sackler family and the company they controlled, Purdue Pharma, manufacturer of the blockbuster opioid drug Oxycontin and a major contributor to the deadly opioid crisis across America. The resolution of lawsuit against Purdue and the Sacklers, will make public tens of millions of documents related to Purdue’s role in the deadly opioid crisis. It also requires the Sacklers personally to pay USD 4,325,000,000 over nine years for prevention, treatment, and recovery efforts in communities across the country.

According to United States Attorney - District of Vermont, United States - Department of Health & Human Services, United States - Department of Justice and United States Attorney - District of New Jersey; November 24, 2020: On November 24, 2020, Opioid company Purdue Pharma LP, pleaded guilty in federal court to conspiracies to defraud the United States and to violate the Anti-Kickback Statute. Purdue pleaded guilty to an Information charging it with three felony offenses, one count of dual-object conspiracy to defraud the United States and to violate the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and two counts of conspiracy to violate the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute.

From May 2007 to March 2017, Purdue conspired to defraud the United States by impeding the lawful function of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The misleading information comprised prescription data that included prescriptions written by doctors that Purdue had good reason to believe were engaged in diversion. The conspiracy also involved aiding and abetting violations of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act by facilitating the dispensing of its opioid products, including OxyContin, without a legitimate medical purpose, and thus without lawful prescriptions. Purdue also admitted it conspired to violate the Anti-Kickback Statute, between June 2009 to March 2017, by making payments to two doctors through Purdue’s physician speaker program to induce those doctors to write more prescriptions for Purdue’s opioid products.

According to United States - Maryland Attorney General, United States - Department of Justice, United States - Department of Health & Human Services, United States Attorney - District of New Jersey, United States Attorney - District of Vermont, United States Attorney - District of Maine and United States Attorney - Eastern District of Texas; October 21, 2020: On October 21, 2020 Purdue Pharma LP,  pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud the United States and to violate the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and two counts of conspiracy to violate the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute. Purdue has also agreed to a civil settlement in the amount of USD 2,800,000,000 to resolve its civil liability under the False Claims Act. Between June 2009 and March 2017, Purdue made payments to two doctors through Purdue’s doctor speaker program to induce those doctors to write more prescriptions of Purdue’s opioid products.  Similarly, from approximately April 2016 through December 2016, Purdue made payments to Practice Fusion Inc., an electronic health records company, in exchange for referring, recommending, and arranging for the ordering of Purdue’s extended-release opioid products – OxyContin, Butrans, and Hysingla.

According to United States - California Attorney General; October 03, 2019: On October 03, 2019, an amended complaint lawsuit against filed against Purdue Pharma, adding eight additional members of the Sackler family. In the lawsuit, it is alleged that Purdue misleadingly introduced OxyContin into the market as a safe and effective treatment for chronic, non-cancer pain. As early as February 1997, Purdue and certain of the Sackler defendants knew that oxycodone-containing drugs like OxyContin were among the most abused opioids in the United States. Yet, between 1996 and 2002, Purdue more than doubled its sales force, and sales rose from approximately USD 48,000,000 to nearly USD 2,000,000,000 in 2002. These sales were made by representatives falsely promoting OxyContin as a drug that was neither addictive nor subject to withdrawal symptoms, while minimizing its potential for abuse and addiction. By March 2000, Purdue was aware of specific reports made to the company about the abuse and diversion of OxyContin occurring in communities across the United States. In fact, in 2007, Purdue and a number of its executives pleaded guilty to felony misbranding of OxyContin, admitting that they illegally promoted OxyContin. Purdue agreed to pay over USD 600,000,000 in criminal and civil penalties, fines, and forfeitures.

Despite this, Purdue continued its deceptive marketing and promoting of OxyContin. Their revenues amounted to USD 3,000,000,000 in 2010, and as much as USD 1,800,000,000 as recently as 2017. The lawsuit further alleges that as part of its aggressive deceptive marketing campaign, Purdue distributed literature and other materials that misrepresented the safety of its opioid products to healthcare professionals and patients in California and elsewhere. Purdue sales representatives further pushed physicians to prescribe opioids to “trusted” patients, and implied that healthcare professionals could screen out potential addicts through urine tests and patient contracts. In addition to the amended complaint, Attorney General also joined a coalition of 23 attorneys general and formally opposed Purdue Pharma’s request to make USD 38,000,000 in bonus, incentive, and other payments to employees.

According to United States - Rhode Island Attorney General, United States - Virginia Attorney General and United States - Pennsylvania Attorney General; September 11, 2019: On September 11, 2019, The State of Rhode Island, by and through its Attorney General, brings this action pursuant to his statutory and common law authority to redress Richard S. Sacker's, Jonathan D. Sackler's, Mortimer D.A. Sackler's, Kathe A. Sackler's, Ilene Sackler Lefcourt's, David A. Sackler's, and Beverly Sackler's (together, the Sacklers) campaign to unlawfully promote and distribute opioids in Rhode Island through their control and use of Purdue Pharma, L.P.'s, Purdue Pharma Inc.'s, the Purdue Frederick Company ( together, Purdue), and the fraudulent transfer of funds generated from such sales to the Sacklers and Prescription opioid are dangerous drugs that have harmed the public health, safety and welfare affecting every community in our State causing the epidemic of opioid addiction and death.

Rhode Island government committed to continuing to aggressively pursue our claims against Purdue Pharma and the Sacklers. On September 11, 2019, filed a complaint against additional members of the Sackler family for the role that they played in the distribution of these highly addictive opioids in Rhode Island.

According to United States - Rhode Island Attorney General; August 16, 2019: Published on that date, The Lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma L.P for pharma trafficking. The lawsuit alleges that defendant opioid manufacturers and distributors knowingly misrepresented the risk posed by prescription opioids in order expand their use and drive-up profits. It is also alleged that, in particular, opioid distributors disregarded obligations to identify suspicious orders and customers, allowing for and failing to stop the diversion of opioids within and to Rhode Island.

According to United States - Arizona Attorney General; July 31, 2019: On July 31, 2019, Lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma LP and others for engaging in deceptive and misleading marketing to push opioids in violation of a 2007 judgment obtained by the Arizona Attorney General’s Office for violating the state’s Consumer Fraud Act.

The defendants allegedly disregarded the judgment and continued to disseminate false, misleading, or unbalanced information through Purdue’s sales representatives, advertising materials, and websites. The State also alleges that they violated the judgment by improperly marketing prescription opioids, including OxyContin, through seemingly independent nonprofits that were paid millions of dollars by Purdue to promote prescription opioids.

According to United States - Nevada Attorney General; June 17, 2019: On June 17, 2019, lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma LP and others for violations of the Nevada Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit alleges that the manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies, and individuals created an ecosystem of addiction with deadly consequences to the state and its residents for their own profit. Through a systematic marketing campaign, sham “medical” organizations, funded experts, and other shameful tactics, the defendant’s peddled false science designed to demonstrate that opioids were a safe, non-addictive treatment for pain. The defendants furthered their wrongful conduct by encouraging doctors to treat addiction with more opioids and intensify the epidemic they created. Even when opioid deaths skyrocketed, the defendants simply redesigned their marketing campaign to continue to reap profits at the expense of Nevadans. Legal causes of action include violations of Nevada’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, False Claims Act, Racketeering Act, negligence, and public nuisance.

The Complaint lists over 40 defendants. Manufacturer defendants include Purdue Pharma LP. Manufacturer Defendants have packaged, distributed, supplied, sold, placed into the stream of commerce, labeled, described, marketed, advertised, promoted and purported to warn or purported to inform prescribers and users regarding the benefits and risks associated with the use of the prescription opioid drugs. 

According to United States - Hawaii Attorney General, United States - Maine Attorney General, United States - California Attorney General and United States - District of Columbia Attorney General; June 03, 2019: Published on that date, Purdue Pharma L.P., Purdue Pharma Inc. (Purdue), certain of its affiliates, and Dr. Richard S. Sackler was sued for unlawful practices in the marketing, sale, and distribution of opioids. The lawsuit alleges that Purdue’s illegal and misleading marketing and sales practices played a major role in contributing to the nationwide opioid crisis. It further alleges that Purdue created a public nuisance through its marketing and sale of opioids and misled healthcare professionals and patients about the addictive nature of opioids and their potential for abuse and diversion.

According to United States - Iowa Attorney General, United States - Maryland Attorney General, United States - Minnesota Attorney General, United States - Oregon Department of Justice Office of the Attorney General and United States - Kansas Attorney General; May 2019: On May 2019,  law suit filed against Purdue Pharma LP for alleging that the drug company engaged in unfair, deceptive and unlawful practices in the marketing of OxyContin, helping fuel the nation’s opioid crisis.

Iowa’s lawsuit, filed in Polk County District Court, seeks restitution and civil penalties under Iowa’s Consumer Fraud Act. It alleges that Purdue, and its related companies Purdue Frederick Co., Purdue Pharmaceuticals and P.F. Laboratories, repeatedly made false and deceptive claims that OxyContin was safe and suitable for a wide range of pain patients. Specifically, the lawsuit alleges that Purdue claimed that OxyContin posed a low risk of addiction; symptoms of addiction were in fact only “pseudoaddiction” indicating the need for more opioids; long-term opioid use improved patients’ quality of life and function; and that opioids were suitable for vulnerable groups, such as elderly patients and veterans. 

According to United States Pennsylvania Attorney General; May 14, 2019: On May 02, 2019, a lawsuit was filed against Purdue Pharma, the creator of prescription painkiller OxyContin, accusing the company of a multi-faceted, illegal effort to market OxyContin in Pennsylvania. Shapiro’s suit is the first to specifically detail Purdue’s barrage of sales representatives targeting Pennsylvania doctors as a key facet of their campaign to push addictive opioids on Pennsylvanians.

The lawsuit alleges that Purdue launched an illegal marketing campaign of deception targeting Pennsylvania doctors and patients to change attitudes, practices, and the culture surrounding pain management. Some of the most egregious components of the campaign include Purdue deployed their highly trained sales staff to blanket Pennsylvania, making sales calls and in-person visits to physicians, totaling more than half a million visits in Pennsylvania alone, an amount second to only California. Purdue targeted Pennsylvania doctors with suspicious prescribing activity and would invest more sales force and marketing to get those doctors to prescribe even more OxyContin – sometimes resulting in as much as a 500% increase in OxyContin prescriptions by one office alone. Purdue misinformed doctors and pharmacists about the addictive nature of OxyContin and used industry thought leaders and in-house marketing literature to dispel the facts about the drug. As the opioid epidemic grew, Purdue created “pseudo-addiction,” a Purdue-conjured disease that showed similar equities as addiction but was to be treated, according to Purdue, with additional opioids. The Office of Attorney General is demanding that the Court issue an order preventing Purdue and anyone associated with Purdue’s misconduct from continuing to engage in these same deceptive tactics. 

According to United States Illinois Attorney General; April 08, 2019: On April 08, 2019, Lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma L.P. and Purdue Pharma Inc. over its deceptive marketing practices designed to significantly increase prescriptions issued for opioids.

According to Raoul, between 2008 and 2017, Purdue dispatched sales representatives to Illinois hundreds of thousands of times. Raoul alleged Purdue also funded third-party publications under the guise of educational materials to promote opioids and downplay their risks, using terms like “pseudo addiction.” Sales representatives informed doctors and patients that the risks could be controlled. Despite knowing that its opioid painkillers were dangerous and being misused and diverted, Purdue allegedly targeted doctors with addicted patients and whose patients were diverting drugs for unlawful use. Raoul alleged that Purdue’s tactics tripled prescriptions of its opioids in Illinois.

According to United States Oklahoma Attorney General and United States New York State Attorney General; March 28, 2019: The lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma LP for engaging in healthcare fraud. 

Pursuant to Executive Law § 63(12), From manufacturing, distributing, selling, or marketing opioids within the State unless it complies with heightened, independently-monitored safeguards against the recurrence of its fraudulent, illegal, and/or unlawful practices, which are to be set forth in a compliance plan reviewed and approved by Plaintiff and the Court.  Pursuant to Executive Law § 63(12), Pay restitution and damages for its fraudulent and/or illegal practices that violated that statute and caused compensable injuries to Plaintiff or any other person; and Disgorge all profits it wrongfully obtained as a result of its fraudulent and/or illegal practices in violation of that statute.

According to United States Tennessee Attorney General; March 26, 2019: On March 26, 2019, The settlement reached against purdue Pharma is a favorable development. After years of denial, Purdue finally recognized its role in creating the opioid crisis.At the same time, a recent Knox County circuit court ruling against Purdue will advance the litigation against the company for violating the state’s Consumer Protection Act. 

According to United States Utah Attorney General; January 30, 2019: The Utah Attorney General’s Office filed an administrative action against Purdue Pharma L.P. and others as part of the State’s efforts to hold accountable the opioid companies and individuals that created and fueled the opioid epidemic throughout Utah.

In the filing, under Utah Code, the Division of Consumer Protection of the Department of Commerce issued an administrative action, in the form of a citation, against the defendants alleging violations of the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act. An administrative proceeding allows the State to seek to prove its claims and obtain a judgment, injunctive relief, and civil penalties more promptly than state district court proceedings. Based on evidence that has emerged over 2018, this administrative action alleges that not only Purdue, but two of its owners also participated in Purdue’s fraudulent conduct.

According to United States Connecticut Attorney General; December 20, 2018: The lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma L.P. and other affiliates for alleging that they designed, financed and waged a pervasive and aggressive campaign to mislead doctors and patients, claiming that prescription opioid medications manufactured and marketed by the company were safe and effective and strategically downplaying risks of addiction that they knew were inherent in their opioid products.

The state alleges that Purdue misinformed patients and doctors to get more and more people taking its premier opioid drug, OxyContin, and its two other opioid medications, Hysingla and Butrans. Purdue allegedly led patients and doctors to believe that opioids were safe to treat even minor pain, and that patients could and should take higher and more dangerous doses. The state alleges that Purdue sent sales representatives to doctors' offices, clinics, pharmacies and hospitals in Connecticut to make deceptive sales pitches about opioid drugs; rewarded high-prescribing doctors with attention, meals, gifts and money; and awarded prizes and bonuses to sales representatives who generated the most opioid prescriptions. In Connecticut, 1038 people died of accidental drug overdoses in 2017, the vast majority from opioid-related overdoses. The Connecticut Office of the Chief Medical Examiner has projected that 1030 more people will die of overdoses in 2018. From 2013 to 2016, Connecticut experienced a fourfold increase in deaths from prescription opioid overdoses, and the estimated economic cost of the opioid epidemic in Connecticut in 2016 was USD 10,270,000,000.

According to US-Florida Attorney General: November 16, 2018: An amended complaint was filed against opioid manufacturers and distributors including Purdue Pharma L.P.

Allegedly, defendants deceptively, unfairly, and unconscionably sought to convince prescribers and patients that opioids are safe, rarely addictive, and necessary for treating a wide range of common ailments. Defendants spread these myths knowing that opioids create physical dependency within days or weeks; that withdrawal from prescription opioids can be agonizing; that long-term and high-dose opioid use is particularly likely to lead to addiction; and that high doses of opioids can be fatal. Defendants at all levels of the supply chain manufacturers, distributors, and chain pharmacies continued selling opioids in Florida even though they knew or should have known that the drugs were being diverted and misused for non-medical purposes. Defendants had duties to identify and stop suspicious orders and purchases, and to put in place reasonable policies to safeguard against diversion.

According to the US-Oregon Department of Justice Office of the Attorney General; September 13, 2018: The complaint alleges that Purdue deceptively marketed OxyContin to Oregon seniors, misrepresented the risks and benefits of the drug, and lied to the Oregon Board of Pharmacy, all to maximize Purdue’s profits. It states that over the last decade Purdue has engaged in a pattern of racketeering and misleading activity in Oregon.

he complaint, filed in Multnomah Circuit Court, details how Purdue’s conduct violated an agreed upon stipulated 2007 Oregon judgment resulting from an earlier investigation of its unlawful practices, as well as four distinct Oregon laws: The Unlawful Trade Practices Act, the Elderly Persons and Persons with Disabilities Abuse Prevention Act, the False Claims Act and the Oregon Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act.

According to the U.S. Rhode Island Attorney General and US-Virginia Attorney General ; June, 2018: On June 25, 2018,  A civil lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma L.P., for prescription opioid manufacturers and distributors over their alleged campaign of unfairly, deceptively, and fraudulently marketing and promoting opioids in Rhode Island.

According to the Complaint, distributors persistently disregarded their obligations to identify suspicious orders and customers, facilitating and failing to stop the diversion of opioids within and to Rhode Island. Rhode Island's Medicaid program spent more than USD 6,000,000 to pay for prescriptions of Purdue-branded opioids, along with additional funds for Purdue's generic opioids and for the costs of providing and using opioids long-term to treat chronic pain.

According to the U.S. Florida Attorney General, U.S. North Dakota Attorney General and U.S. Texas Attorney General; May 15, 2018: A lawsuit was filed against Purdue Pharma L.P. for allegedly using a campaign of misrepresentations and omissions about the use of opioids to doctors and consumers in order to increase prescriptions and opioid use, including false statements about the addictive nature of opioids and omissions of the severe risks posed by taking opioids. 

The opioid distributors allegedly shipped inordinately high volumes of opioids to customers in Florida and failed to report these suspicious orders of opioids, thereby fueling widespread diversion of opioids throughout the state. In the complaint filed the defendants’ actions violated the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, the Florida RICO Act, and violated common law public nuisance and negligence. 

According to the US-Delaware Attorney General and the Department of Justice; January 19, 2018: On January 19, 2018 A lawsuit filed against Purdue Pharma LP  for engaging in false, deceptive and unfair marketing of prescription opioids.

Purdue Pharma LP engaged, and continue to engage, in a massive marketing campaign to misstate and conceal the risks of treating chronic pain with opioids. Although manufacturers are prohibited from marketing opioids through misstatements or omissions of material facts, Manufacturer Defendants nonetheless disseminated misstatements through multiple channels. This campaign includes websites, promotional materials, conferences, guidelines for doctors, and other vehicles. 

Purdue Pharma L.P. (together with Purdue Pharma Inc. and The Purdue Frederick Company, “Purdue”) is a limited partnership organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware with its principal place of business located in Stamford, Connecticut. During all relevant times, Purdue Pharma L.P. has manufactured and distributed substantial amounts of prescription opioids that have been and continue to be sold in Delaware. Purdue Pharma L.P. has engaged in consensual commercial dealings with Delaware and its citizens, and has purposefully availed itself of the advantages of conducting business with and within Delaware.

row.profile_notes:
On July 25, 2018, the United States Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control imposed sanctions against Anni Beurklian. Anni Beurklian was a key component of a vast network procuring electronics on behalf of Syria’s Scientific Studies and Research Center (SSRC), the agency responsible for the development of Syria’s chemical weapons.

According to United States United States Attorney - District of Massachusetts; June 11, 2020: On June 11, 2020, filed a civil forfeiture action against Anni Beurklian and her husband Antoine Ajaka in connection with a scheme to smuggle goods out of the United States and to supply services to Syria. The United States also seized the U.S. website of the Syrian-based company Electronic Katranji Trading (“EKT”), ekt2.com, on probable cause that it was used to facilitate the illegal export of merchandise from the United States.The couple operated Top Tech US Inc. (“Top Tech”), a U.S. company, from the Waltham home. Beurklian, Ajaka and Top Tech were indicted in March 2018 on conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws and regulations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, smuggling U.S. goods out of the United States, illegally providing services to persons located in Syria, mail fraud, conspiracy to obstruct justice and obstruction of justice.

The civil forfeiture action and website seizure are pursuant to Title 19 of the United States Code, which provides that property used to facilitate the exporting or sending of merchandise from the United States contrary to law shall be seized and forfeited to the United States.

According to United States Department of State Directorate of Defense Trade Controls; November, 2019: On March 21, 2018 Anni Beurkl and her husband, Antoine Ajaka their company Top Tech US Inc, and a Syrian national Amir Katranji were indicted on conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws and regulations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, smuggling U.S. goods out of the United States, conspiracy to obstruct justice, and obstruction of justice. Beurklian, Ajaka, and Top Tech US Inc. also are charged with illegally providing services to persons located in Syria and mail fraud.

According to United States Attorney - District of Massachusetts; March 21, 2018: Anni Beurklian and her husband, Antoine Ajaka, their company Top Tech US Inc, and a Syrian national Amir Katranji were indicted on conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws and regulations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, smuggling U.S. goods out of the United States, conspiracy to obstruct justice, and obstruction of justice. Beurklian, Ajaka, and Top Tech US Inc. are also charged with illegally providing services to persons located in Syria and mail fraud. Beurklian and Ajaka previously fled the U.S. and have not returned. 

As alleged in the indictment, beginning no later than 2012 and continuing until Jan. 09, 2018, Beurklian and her husband operated an export business, Top Tech US Inc., out of their Waltham residence. The couple used their business to procure goods, including electronics, computer equipment, and electrical switches, from U.S. companies and export those goods out of the United States to customers in Lebanon and Syria. 

The indictment further alleges that in or about 2013, Ajaka and Beurklian began doing business with Katranji and supplying U.S. origin goods to EKT using Top Tech US. Ajaka and Beurklian knew that Katranji operated a business in Syria and that they were providing brokering services to Katranji and his Syrian company, EKT, by buying and shipping U.S. origin goods to EKT and its customers. EKT paid Ajaka and Beurklian more than USD 200,000 through Top Tech US bank accounts for their services. To conceal their illegal activity with EKT and evade the mandatory export filing requirement, Ajaka and Beurklian, with the knowledge and agreement of Katranji, falsified shipping paperwork and undervalued goods being shipped overseas directly to, or on behalf of, EKT.

row.profile_notes:
On May 15, 2025, the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs imposed sanctions against Omar Ali Hussain.

On June 04, 2021, the Minister of State of Monaco imposed sanctions against Omar Ali HUSSAIN.

On December 31, 2020, the United Kingdom Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office designated OMAR ALI HUSSAIN.

On November 24, 2016, the Trinidad and Tobago Financial Intelligence Unit listed OMAR on its Targeted Financial Sanctions List.

On March 17, 2016, OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to the Indonesian Financial Transaction Reports and Analysis Center Suspected Terrorists and Terrorist Organizations list.

On September 29, 2015, the United States Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control designated Omar HUSSAIN under the Specially Designated Nationals List.

On September 28, 2015, the Council of the European Union imposed sanctions on Omar Ali Hussain regarding Regulation 2015/1815 imposing certain specific restrictive measures directed against certain persons and entities associated with the Al-Qaida network.

On September 18, 2015, the United Nations Security Council imposed sanctions against Omar Ali Hussain for being a foreign fighter for the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant. UK national Hussain was considered to be one of ISIL’s most prominent recruiters. As an ISIL fighter, he offered tips on evading British security to individuals interested in leaving the United Kingdom to fight with ISIL.

On September 28, 2015, Omar Ali HUSSAIN was added to the New Zealand Police List as a designated terrorist entity.

On September 28, 2015, OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority regarding ISIL and Al-Qaida.

On September 28, 2015, Omar Ali Hussain was added to the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade Financial Sanction List.

On September 28, 2015, OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was sanctioned by the President of the Governorate of the Vatican City State.

On September 28, 2015, OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to South Africa's Targeted Financial Sanctions List.

On September 28, 2015, OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to Argentina Registro Público de Personas y Entidades Vinculadas a Actos de Terrorismo y su Financiamiento List.

The Ministry of Economy and Finance of France imposed sanctions against Omar Ali HUSSAIN.

OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was sanctioned by the State Financial Monitoring Service of Ukraine.

The Ministry of Finance of Japan sanctioned OMAR ALI HUSSAIN.

OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to Liechtenstein's Financial Market Authority sanctions list regarding Al-Qaida.

OMAR  ALI HUSSAIN was added to Israel Ministry of Defense Sanction List.

OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to the Financial Intelligence Unit of Mexico Sanction list 1267- ISIL & Al-Qaida.

The State Security Agency of Belarus Included Ali Hussain Omar in the list of individuals and organizations involved in terrorism.

OMAR ALI HUSSAIN was added to the Turkey Ministry Decisions Regarding Article 5 of Law 6415 List.

According to Macao Asset Freezing Coordination Commission; February 18, 2020: The Macao Asset Freezing Coordination Commission added Omar Ali Hussain onto its asset freeze list in pursuant of UN Resolution 1267 (1999) on February 18, 2020.

According to Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financial Anti-Terrorist Financing Ministerial Regulations from Luxembourg; October 01, 2015: On September 29, 2015, the Ministry of Finance from Luxembourg reported that Omar Ali Hussain was added on the list of entities subjected to assets freeze.

According to United States Attorney - District of South Carolina, United States Department of Health & Human Services and United States Department of Justice; March 06, 2025: Published on that date, Omar Hussain and his marketing company agreed to pay USD 817,808 to resolve allegations that from April 2020 to August 2021, Hussain and his company received commissions from the South Carolina laboratory as independent contractors based on the volume and/or value of the Medicare and TRICARE referrals for laboratory testing that they arranged for and/or recommended.

row.profile_notes:
According to U.S. Federal Trade Commission; December 11, 2019: On December 06, 2019 Omar Hussain and others were ordered to pay jointly and severally USD 8,877,564 for engaging in deceptive practice. The defendants were permanently banned from the debt collection business and from misleading consumers about debt in a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission. In addition to being banned from debt collection, debt brokering activities, and misleading consumers, the defendants also will be banned from misrepresenting to consumers whether they are attorneys.

According to U.S. Federal Trade Commission; February 08, 2019: On February 04, 2019, a federal court has temporarily halted and frozen the assets of a debt collection scheme that allegedly bilked consumers out of millions of dollars, using deceptive and threatening tactics to collect phantom debts that they did not owe. Omar Hussain and others falsely claimed to be attorneys or affiliated with attorneys to pressure consumers into making payments on debts they did not owe, and threatened to take legal action against consumers if they did not pay. The complaint charged that the Omar Hussain deceptive and unfair tactics violated the FTC Act and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. Hussain is or was a manager, director, president, or organizer of Trans America, Midwestern Alliance, TACS I,  TACS II , TACS III, and Cedar Rose. He is or was an authorized signatory on the bank and merchant accounts for many of the Defendants. At all times material to this complaint, acting alone or in concert with others, he has formulated, directed, controlled, had the authority to control, or participated in the acts and practices set forth in this Complaint.
