row.profile_notes:
According to United States-Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; December 1998:
Name: James G. Oliver
Address: Grapeville, Texas
Action: Individuals Whose Registrations Were Revoked for Failure to Pay Fines, Costs And/Or Provide Proof of Restitution in Connection with Violations
Action Date: October 27, 1998

According to United States –Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; January 1997: On November 19, 1996, Peter Dennis Mathews, James Gus Oliver, Robert Alan Williky, Mark Joseph Vanyo, Lyle Emery Bettenhausen, Sr. and Gloria Ann Williams. Mathews, Oliver, Williky, Vanyo, and Bettenhausen submitted an Offer of Settlement pursuant to which Oliver was fined USD 25,000, suspended from association with any NASD member in any capacity for 90 days, and required to requalify by exam. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Mathews, Oliver, Williky, Vanyo, and Bettenhausen consented to the described sanctions and to the entry of findings that, in connection with a public offering, Mathews and Williky knowingly effected transactions that they knew or should have known, or were reckless in not knowing, were non-bona fide and designed to create the appearance of a successful completion of the offering. 

The findings also stated that Mathews and Williky knowingly or recklessly bid for and purchased, induced orders to bid for and purchase, and sold or resold, 20 percent of the offering while the distribution continued after its purported closing. Furthermore, the NASD determined that Mathews, Oliver, and Vanyo, by means of manipulative, deceptive, and other fraudulent devices and contrivances, effected a series of transactions that created actual and apparent trading in a stock, artificially supported the price, and were effected for the purpose of inducing the purchase or sale of the stock to others. The NASD found that Mathews, Oliver, and Bettenhausen made statements of material fact that they knew, had reason to know, or were reckless in not knowing, were false to induce retail customers to make investment decisions. The NASD also determined that Mathews executed transactions in the accounts of public customers that were not authorized and were made in order to support a stock price, further the aforementioned manipulative scheme, and avoid net capital deficiencies by lowering his member firm’s inventory. The findings stated that Mathews also allowed an individual, who was precluded from functioning as a registered representative, to direct trading, update quotations, direct unauthorized transactions in customer accounts, and participate in selling group and retail sales efforts at his member firm. The individual also failed to establish, maintain, and enforce supervisory procedures to assure compliance with applicable rules, misused customer funds, and engaged in private securities transactions.

row.details: enforcement: Tax Evasion/Wire Fraud/Money Laundering/Conspiracy/Stolen Property | US-U.S. Department of Justice | United States || Tax Evasion/Fraud | US-U.S. Courts | United States

row.profile_notes:
Mark Edward Whitacre was born on 1 May 1957.

According to the U.S. Courts; On March4, 1998, Mark E Whitacre was imprisoned for a term of ten and half years in prison for fraud and tax fraud. He is to pay restitution in the sum of $11,403,698.00. On July 9, 1999, Mark E Whitacre was imprisoned for a total term of thirty (30) months. Upon release from imprisonment the defendant shall be on supervised release for a term of one (1) year for violations affecting interstate commerce. 

According to the U.S. Department of Justice; January 15, 1997: A federal grand jury indicted Mark E. Whitacre, a former vice president of Archer Daniels Midland Company, on charges of wire fraud, interstate transportation of stolen property, money laundering, forfeiture, conspiracy, obstruction of justice, and filing false income tax returns.

The indictment charges Whitacre with conducting a scheme to defraud and obtain more than $9 million from his former employer where he served as president of its Bioproducts division and as a vice president of the parent company until the summer of 1995. The indictment charges that from the spring of 1991, and continuing through November 1995, Whitacre defrauded the money from ADM and laundered the proceeds of his frauds through the use of foreign and domestic companies and bank accounts, including accounts established in the Cayman Islands, Germany, Hong Kong and Switzerland.

The indictment further charges that Whitacre conspired with another to defraud the United States for the purpose of obstructing and defeating the ascertainment and collection of income taxes by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and that he filed false income tax returns with the IRS for the tax years 1991 through 1994. The indictment further charges Whitacre with obstructing justice by attempting to corruptly persuade a witness to provide misleading information to federal law enforcement officials. In December 1996 a Chicago federal grand jury indicted Whitacre and two other former top ADM officials for conspiring to fix prices and allocate sales in the lysine market worldwide.

According to the pina.com.fj; June 13, 2013: On June 12, 2013, Timothy Pangelinan Villagomez, former Lieutenant Governor of the Northern Mariana Islands, was resentenced to hundred and eight months imprisonment, or nine years, from the original eighty seven months for his role in the Rydlyme corruption scandal. After an 18-day trial almost four years ago, Villagomez was convicted of conspiracy to defraud the United States, wire fraud, theft concerning a program receiving federal funds, and bribery concerning a program receiving federal funds that involved the Commonwealth Utilities Corp.

According to the saipantribune.com; August 06, 2009: On August 05, 2009, Timothy Pangelinan Villagomez, former Lieutenant Governor, was sentenced to eighty seven months in prison and three years of supervised release for his role in the Rydlyme corruption scandal. Judge ordered Villagomez and the Santos couple to jointly pay USD 346,125 to the court for reimbursement to CUC. Judge also ordered Villagomez and the Santos couple to each pay a USD 400 court assessment fee and perform 200 hours of community service. Villagomez and the Santos couple were found guilty on April 24, 2009, of all charges relating to CUC's purchases of excessive amounts of a chemical, at a 400 percent markup, from companies owned by James and Joaquina Santos.

According to the saipantribune.com; August 12, 2008: On August 11, 2008, Former Lt. Gov. Timothy Villagomez entered a federal court in handcuffs to face an indictment on three felony counts of wire fraud, conspiracy and theft of federal funds, the culmination of an extensive five-month investigation by federal authorities. The indictment, charges Villagomez, Commerce Secretary James Santos, his wife Joaquina Santos-who is Villagomez's sister-and former Commonwealth Utilities Corp. executive director Anthony Guerrero with conspiring to bilk the CNMI government out of thousands of dollars through business deals involving needless chemical purchases for CUC. Villagomez and the Santos' pleaded not guilty to each of the charges against them.

According to leparisien.fr; April 28, 2026: Lafarge SA as well as its eight co-defendants appealed the decision of the Paris Court delivered on April 13, 2026. 

According to lemonde.fr; April 13, 2026: On April 13, 2026, the Criminal Court of Paris sentenced Lafarge to a EUR 1 125 000 fine for financing terrorism. The court also imposed a customs fine of EUR 4 500 000 for embargo violations to be paid jointly with other defendants. The French cement company Lafarge and its executives were found guilty of paying nearly EUR 5 600 000 to terrorist groups, including ISIS, and intermediaries in Syria between 2013 and 2014 to maintain its business operations in the area. 

According to midilibre.fr; December 19, 2025: The verdict for Lafarge SA in the financing terrorism case will be announced on April 13, 2026. 

According to lemonde.fr; December 16, 2025: On December 16, 2025, the prosecution requested a EUR 1 125 000 fine for Lafarge SA along with a partial confiscation of assets totaling EUR 30 000,000 as part of the trial for financing terrorism. Lafarge SA and four senior executives are also being prosecuted for failure to comply with international financial sanctions. In that part of the case, the prosecution has sought a joint customs fine of EUR 4 570,000.

According to actu-juridique.fr; November 18, 2025: The trial of Lafarge and its eight former executives accused of financing terrorism resumed on November 18, 2025, in Paris. It will last until December 19, 2025.

According to lefigaro.fr; November 06, 2025: The trial of Lafarge SA accused of financing terrorism was rescheduled to start on November 18, 2025.

According to lemonde.fr and lexpress.fr; October 16, 2024: On October 16, 2024, Lafarge SA and eight individuals were sent to trial for financing terrorism. In this case Lafarge is suspected of having paid EUR 5 000 000 to terrorist groups, including ISIS, and intermediaries to maintain its activities in Jalabiya between 2013 and 2014. According to the provisional calendar, the trial was scheduled to be held from November 04, 2025 till December 09, 2025.
Within another part of the case, Lafarge SA remains under investigation for crimes against humanity. 

According to lemonde.fr; February 09, 2024: On February 09, 2024, the French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office submitted a request to bring Lafarge SA and nine individuals to trial on charges of financing terrorist groups. The accusations relate to the activities of Lafarge SA in Syria in 2013-2014. Lafarge SA has already admitted paying about EUR 13 000 000 to different intermediaries in order to keep its Syrian cement factory running at that time; however, the company claimed no responsibility for the money eventually coming to the terrorist groups, allegedly including ISIS.

According to leparisien.fr; January 16, 2024: The Court of Cassation upheld the decision to place Lafarge under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity. The decision is final. The company also stays under investigation for terrorism financing allegedly committed between 2013 and 2014 in Syria. 

According to zonebourse.com; November 23, 2023: The decision of the French Cassation Court, concerning the appeal of Lafarge to drop complicity in crimes against humanity charges, has been postponed until January 16, 2024.

According to sudouest.fr; January 24, 2023: Lafarge SA has appealed before the Cassation Court the decision of the Appeal Court of Paris to place Lafarge SA under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity regarding its activities in Syria before 2014. Lafarge SA is suspected of having paid millions of dollars to jihadist groups and intermediaries to maintain its cement works in Syria between 2013 and 2014. The Cassation Court scheduled to announce its verdict on March 14, 2023.

According to United States - Department of Justice and United States Attorney - Eastern District of New York; October 18, 2022: On October 18, 2022, Lafarge S.A. and and Lafarge Cement Syria, S.A. (LCS) pleaded guilty to a one-count criminal information charging them with conspiring to provide material support and resources to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) and the al-Nusrah Front (ANF), both U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. The defendants were sentenced to three year term of probation and to pay financial penalties, including criminal fines of USD 90 780 000 and forfeiture of USD 687 000 000 totaling USD 777 780 000. The defendants’ scheme to pay ISIS and ANF in exchange for permission to operate a cement plant in Syria from August 2013 to October 2014, which enabled LCS to obtain approximately USD 70 300 000 in revenue. 

As a result of the scheme, LCS obtained approximately USD 70 300 000 in total sales revenue from August 2013 through 2014.  The gains to all participants in the conspiracy, including LCS, the intermediaries and the terrorist groups, totaled approximately USD 80 540 000.

According to france24.com; May 18, 2022: On May 18, 2022, the Appeal Court of Paris upheld the decision to place Lafarge SA under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity.

According to lefigaro.fr; March 24, 2022: On March 24, 2022, the Appeal Court of Paris heard the case of Lafarge SA regarding the complicity in crimes against humanity. The decision will be announced on May 18, 2022. In 2018, the company was formally placed under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity; however, in November 2019, the Paris Appeal Court canceled that decision. Then, in September 2021, the Cassation Court canceled the decision of the Appeal Court and sent the case back to the investigating chamber. The prosecution demands to place Lafarge SA under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity as it, allegedly, financed via its subsidiaries the activities of ISIS.  

According to leparisien.fr; November 07, 2019: Lafarge SA is still under investigation for terrorism financing and putting the lives of others in danger in relation to its business activities in Syria. 

According to lemonde.fr and lepoint.fr; June 28, 2018: On June 28, 2018, Lafarge SA was placed under formal investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity and financing terrorist undertaking. Lafarge SA was placed under judicial supervision comprising a EUR 30 000 000 bail. Allegedly, between 2011 and 2015, Lafarge paid EUR 13 000 000 to the terrorist groups in order to maintain its business activities in Syria. 

According to leparisien.fr; June 13, 2017: On June 09, 2017, the Prosecutor's Office of Paris launched a judicial inquiry for the alleged financing of a terrorist undertaking and putting the lives of others in danger, possibly implicating LafargeHolcim. Reportedly, LafargeHolcim might have been indirectly providing funds to the armed groups in Syria. In March 2017, French company Lafarge (now renamed LafargeHolcim after a merger) admitted to indirectly financing armed groups in Syria between 2013 and 2014 in order to maintain its business activities. 

According to francais.rt.com; January 19, 2017: In September 2016, the Ministry of the Economy asked a court to investigate possible violations committed by the cement group Lafarge in Syria in relation to the prohibition to buy oil in this country enacted by the European Union in 2012. The Paris public prosecutor's office opened a preliminary investigation on these allegations in October 2016.
The French cement company is also suspected of having concluded agreements with the Islamic State. These allegations are contained in a complaint filed by NGO Sherpa in November 2016. Lafarge reportedly concluded a series of agreements with several armed groups, including the Islamic State, in order to continue its activity in northeastern Syria. These agreements allegedly reached in 2013 allowed it to continue operating its cement plant in Jalabiya before it was taken by Daesh in 2014.

According to United States - Illinois State Board of Investment; In 2018, Lafarge SA was removed from the Illinois State Board of Investment restricted list for having ties with Government of Sudan. 

According to the European Commission; March 14, 2014: In December 2010, the European Commission (EC) launched antitrust proceedings against a number of cement manufacturers for suspected breaches of EU rules banning restrictive business practices. The Commission is investigating possible import/export restrictions, market sharing and price coordination in the markets for cement, cement-based products (e.g., ready mix concrete) and other materials used to produce cement-based products (e.g., clinker, aggregates, blast-furnace slag, granulated blast-furnace slag, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, fly ash). One of the suspected companies is Lafarge.

According to United States - Illinois State Board of Investment: As of June 30, 2011 Lafarge SA was included in the prohibited list, deemed prohibited from investment for having ties with Government of Sudan. 

According to khl.com; December 10, 2010: The European Commission (EC) has launched antitrust proceedings against seven cement manufacturers active in member states. The formal proceedings were launched over suspicions that the companies acted to restrict trade flows in the European Economic Area, including organizing import and export restrictions. The alleged cartel is said to have colluded in market sharing and price fixing in the markets for cement and cement-based materials such as ready-mix concrete, clinker, aggregates, blast-furnace slag, granulated blast-furnace slag, ground granulated blast-furnace slag and fly ash. Cemex, Holcim and Heidelberg have so far confirmed that they are under investigation, while reports have cited Lafarge and Dyckerhoff as among those suspected by the EC of colluding with rivals in order to fix prices in Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK.

According to eur-lex.europa.eu; June 17, 2010: On June 17, 2010, the European Union's highest court has upheld a EUR 249,600,000 penalty imposed on Lafarge SA by the European Commission in November 2002. The European Court of Justice dismissed Lafarge’s appeal for an annulment of a reduction of its fine in its entirety.

According to the European Commission; July 08, 2008: The Court of First Instance confirmed the existence and duration of the cartel and upheld the fines imposed on all but one addressee (BPB PLC). On November 27, 2002, the Commission fined BPB PLC (United Kingdom), Gebrüder Knauf Westdeutsche Gipswerke KG (Germany), Société Lafarge SA (France) and Gyproc Benelux SA/NV (Belgium) for participating in a cartel on the market for plasterboard, a product which is widely used in the building industry and by DIY practitioners, in the United Kingdom, Germany, France and the Benelux countries between 1992 and 1998.

According to aachener-zeitung.de; February 18, 2007: Six cement makers face a court ruling in Germany on whether a group of customers can claim damages to the tune of EUR 100 000 000 (USD 133 000 000) if the companies are found guilty of price fixing. The claims stem from an investigation and subsequent fines handed to the cement makers by the country’s Federal Cartel Office in 2003 after it uncovered evidence of price fixing. The companies involved in the case are Dyckerhoff AG, HeidelbergCement AG, Holcim Ltd of Switzerland and Schwenk Zement KG of Germany as well as Lafarge SA of France and Ireland’s Readymix Plc, now owned by Cemex SA.

According to Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa; February 23, 2004: In February 2004, the Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa annulled the tender offers for the exchange of Lafarge bonds. It had previously suspended the offer, which had been made in Italy via the a central securities depository for 90 days as a precautionary measure. 

According to Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa; November 24, 2003: In November 2003, the Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa ordered the preventive suspension for 90 days of the exchange offer for Lafarge bonds. The orders are based on the fact that the Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa has no record of having received either notice of such a public offer or the information document to be published, as required by the Italian law.

According to European Commission; November 27, 2002: The European Commission imposed fines totaling EUR 478 000 000 on four companies which operated a long-running cartel on the market for plasterboard, a product which is widely used in the building industry and by DIY practitioners. The cartel affected 80% of consumers in the European Union, namely in France, the United Kingdom, Germany and the Benelux countries. Two of the companies involved, Lafarge and BPB, were committing their second infringement of EU law on restrictive agreements, having already been fined once in 1994. The Commission has consequently decided to impose the fines totaling EUR 249 600,000 on Lafarge SA.

According to curia.europa.eu; March 15, 2000: Lafarge Coppée SA had its fine reduced from EUR 23 900 000 to EUR 14 248 000 by the judgment of the Court of First Instance.

According to European Commission; November 30, 1994: The European Commission decided to impose fines on the European Cement Association (Cembureau), eight national cement associations and 33 European cement producers for infringements of Article 85 of the EC Treaty involving their participation from 1983 in a general market-sharing agreement, transnational restrictive practices and restrictive practices relating to exports (market sharing and exchanges of information). The firms concerned are based in all the Member States and in some of the EFTA  countries  (Norway, Sweden and Switzerland).
Lafarge Coppée S.A. was imposed fines totaling EUR 23 900 000.

Description:
Lafarge SA, a French cement company, merged with Swiss company Holcim to create LafargeHolcim in July 2015. Lafarge SA continued its activity as a wholly-owned subsidiary of LafargeHolcim.

According to United States - Environmental Protection Agency; March 04, 2026: On March 04, 2026, A complaint filed against Canada Holdings LLC (F/k/a Lafarge North America, Inc. and others alleging each of the defendants own or operate, owned or operated, or arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances for, at least one facility and/or vessel at the Site as defined in Section 101(9) & (28) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(9) & (28) and RCW 70A.305.020(24). 

The United States has undertaken response actions to address the release or threatened release of hazardous substances at or from the Site. In undertaking the response actions, the United States has incurred and will continue to incur response costs as defined in Section 101(25) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(25). EPA has determined that the hazardous substances at the Site present significant risks to human health and the environment, and that response actions are necessary to abate a danger or threat.

According to United States Attorney - Western District of New York; October 31, 2012: Published on that date, Lafarge North America, Inc., (LNA), a national supplier of building and construction materials and manufacturer of concrete and concrete products, has paid USD 950,000 to the United States to resolve potential civil claims by the United States under the False Claims Act. 

The matter involved highway construction projects in the Western District of New York which were funded, in part, by federal funds via the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). This required that a certain percentage of the work be performed by Disadvantaged Business Enterprises (DBE). Rayford Enterprises, Inc., d/b/a Rayford Concrete Products, a Buffalo company, was awarded subcontracts on these construction projects based on its representations that it was a DBE manufacturer of concrete. Rayford was not, in fact, a manufacturer of concrete, nor did the company have a concrete batching facility or other equipment necessary to manufacture concrete. Instead, Rayford had an agreement with Lafarge North America to manufacture and deliver concrete for these projects. Lafarge North America is not a DBE.

According to United States Department of Justice and United States Environmental Protection Agency; November 29, 2011: Published on that date, Lafarge North America Inc. agrees to pay USD 740,000 Penalty to Resolve Clean Water Act Violations in Five States. Lafarge North America Inc., one of the largest suppliers of construction materials in the United States and Canada, and four of its U.S. subsidiaries have agreed to resolve alleged Clean Water Act violations. The violations include unpermitted discharges of stormwater and failure to comply with stormwater permits at 21 stone, gravel, sand, asphalt and ready-mix concrete facilities in Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Maryland and New York.  Stormwater flowing over concrete manufacturing facilities can carry debris, sediment and pollutants including pesticides, petroleum products, chemicals and solvents, which can have a significant impact on water quality.

Lafarge will implement a nationwide evaluation and compliance program at 189 of its similar facilities in the United States to ensure they meet Clean Water Act requirements. Lafarge will also pay a penalty of USD 740,000 and implement two supplemental environmental projects, in which the company will complete conservation easements to protect approximately 166 acres in Maryland and Colorado. The value of the land has been appraised at USD 2,950,000. Lafarge will also implement one state environmentally beneficial project to support environmental training for state inspectors. The state project is valued at USD 10,000.

According to United States Environmental Protection Agency; January 21, 2010: On January 21, 2015, United States filed Clean Air Act settlement with Lafarge North America, Inc. to reduce air emissions from container glass and Portland cement plants throughout the country. The settlements covers all 13 U.S. plants owned by the Lafarge Company and two subsidiaries, the nation’s second largest manufacturer of Portland cement.

Lafarge has also agreed to pay a civil penalty of USD 5,075,000 within 30 days of entry of the consent decree. USD 3,383,000 will be paid to the United States, and the remainder will be paid to the state and local agencies participating in the settlement.

According to United States - Maryland Attorney General; May 13, 2009: Published on that date, the State of Maryland has filed suit against Lafarge North America for water pollution violations at its Texas Quarry in Cockeysville. The complaint filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County alleges 413 violations of Maryland’s water pollution laws at the concrete production and limestone quarry. Each violation carries a maximum penalty of USD 10,000.

The Texas Quarry is a surface mine operated by Lafarge and mined primarily for construction aggregate. On or about March 21, 2007, it is alleged that Lafarge discharged several tons of aggregate, crushed stone, and stone dust into nearby Goodwin Run a tributary of Gunpowder Falls and its floodplain. The amount of material discharged ranged in depth from four to 18 inches and reduced the width of the stream from approximately 15 feet wide to less than four feet wide.

row.position_or_allegation: Agreed to pay USD 1,500,000 for engaging in environmental crimes - September 28, 2000.
row.details: enforcement: Environmental Crimes/Disciplined | US-U.S. Federal Trade Commission | United States
row.profile_notes:
According to United Stated-Michigan Attorney General; September 28, 2000: On September 28, 2000, The Department of Environmental Quality, Michigan announced that the Lafarge Corporation has agreed to settle an air pollution enforcement action resulting from the operation of its Portland cement manufacturing plant in Alpena. As a result of the settlement, the company has agreed to reduce emissions of hydrogen chloride (HCl) from its Portland cement kilns and to control dust levels around the facility.

Lafarge will pay more than USD 1,500,000 to install the control measures required by the settlement and will pay the State of Michigan USD 723,000 in penalties and fines.

According to United Stated-Federal Trade Commission; October 16, 1998: On October 16, 1998, LaFarge, Corp. has agreed to restructure its agreement to purchase certain assets of Holnam, Inc., to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that the purchase agreement violated federal antitrust laws and could drive up prices for cement in the Pacific Northwest. LaFarge Corp. is based in Reston, Virginia. It is one of the largest suppliers of cement for residential, commercial, institutional and public works construction, with 14 plants in the United States and Canada and sales of USD 1600000 in 1996. Holnam, headquartered in Dundee, Michigan, is the number one supplier of cement in the United States. It operates 19 cement plants in North America and had sales of USD 983000000 in 1996.

According to United Stated-Federal Trade Commission; October 16, 1998: On October 16, 1998, The Federal Trade Commission issued Complaint against Lafarge, S.A  having reason to believe that the Lafarge, S.A controls, Lafarge Corporation (collectively "Respondents"), has entered into an agreement to acquire cement production assets of Holnam, Inc., that the agreement violates Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as amended, 15 U.S.C.  45, and that the acquisition, if consummated, would result in a violation of Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as amended, 15 U.S.C. 45, and Section 7 of the Clayton Act, as amended, 15 U.S.C.  18, and it appearing to the Commission that a proceeding in respect thereof would be in the public interest, hereby issues its complaint,

THE PROPOSED ACQUISITION: On February 4, 1998, Lafarge and Holnam signed a Letter of Intent setting out the principal elements of a proposed transaction, whereby Lafarge would acquire Holnam's Seattle, Washington cement plant and related assets.

row.profile_notes:
According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; January 21, 2010: The United States today filed two major Clean Air Act settlements to reduce air emissions from container glass and Portland cement plants throughout the country, announced Cynthia Giles, assistant administrator for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Enforcement and Compliance Assurance and Ignacia S. Moreno, Assistant Attorney General for the Environment and Natural Resources Division. The settlements cover 15 U.S. plants owned by Saint-Gobain Containers, Inc., the nation’s second largest container glass manufacturer, and all 13 U.S. plants owned by the Lafarge Company and two subsidiaries, the nation’s second largest manufacturer of Portland cement. These settlements are the first system-wide settlements for these sectors under the Clean Air Act and require pollution control upgrades, acceptance of enforceable emission limits and payment of civil penalties.

Lafarge has also agreed to pay a civil penalty of USD 5,075,000 within 30 days of entry of the consent decree. USD 3,383,000 will be paid to the United States, and the remainder will be paid to the state and local agencies participating in the settlement.

row.profile_notes: Description: On March 1, 1968, The New York State Legislature created the Metropolitan Transportation Authority to oversee transportation operations in 12 counties. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority is the public benefit corporation of the State of New York responsible for an integrated mass transportation system for the City of New York and Dutchess, Nassau, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Suffolk and Westchester counties. The statutory purposes set forth in the MTA enabling act are: the continuance, further development and improvement of commuter transportation and other services related thereto within the metropolitan commuter transportation district, including but not limited to such transportation by railroad, omnibus, marine and air, in accordance with the provisions of this title. It is governed by a 23-member Board of Directors, whose members are appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the State Senate.

row.profile_notes:
According to the roscommonherald.ie; August 10, 2022: On August 10, 2022, Farah Damji was arrested on by gardaí at a property in rural Co Galway before being brought before the vacation sitting of the High Court in Dublin. The High Court has remanded Damji in custody, who is wanted in the UK to serve out the remainder of her prison sentence for stalking and breaching a restraining order. She has several fraud convictions in a number of jurisdictions, was arrested on foot of a bench warrant issued over her alleged failure to appear before courts that were considering the extradition request.

According to the independent.ie; June 28, 2022: In June 2022, A bench warrant has been issued for the arrest of notorious international conwoman Farah Damji, who lost a Supreme Court bid to prevent her extradition to the UK and has failed to appear before a scheduled sitting of the High Court.

According to the roscommonherald.ie; June 16, 2022: In June 2022, Supreme court upholds decision to extradite on-the-run fraudster Farah Damji to the UK. She will be extradited to the United Kingdom to serve the remainder of her sentence for stalking-type offences and breaching a restraining order after the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal.

According to the irishtimes.com; January 31, 2022: The High Court has ordered the extradition of on-the-run fraudster Farah Damji to the UK, where she is wanted for fleeing a trial. She has been remanded on continuing bail, as the court heard she intends to appeal the decision.

According to the irishtimes.com; August 17, 2020: On August 17, 2020, Farah Damji also known as Farah Dan, was arrested in Dublin. A search was carried out at a block of apartments in Dublin’s north inner city, close to Bachelor’s Walk, where she was located and arrested. She had fled to Ireland while on the run amid a trial in London in which she was convicted and sentenced in her absence. She was convicted in February on two counts of breaching a restraining order, in April 2018 and June 2018. Following her conviction in her absence, she was sentenced in March to 27 months in jail and a European Arrest Warrant was issued for her. She has a long and storied criminal career stretching back to the early 1990s, when she ran an art gallery in New York and East Hampton.

According to the dailymail.co.uk; January 29, 2010: On January 29, 2010, Farah Damji, daughter of multi-millionaire property tycoon Amir Damji, was sentenced to 15 months in prison for a GBP 17,500 housing benefit fraud. She admitted three counts of dishonestly making false representations to Hammersmith and Fulham Council, a letting agency and a landlord. She had already served for three-and-a-half years after being found guilty at Blackfriars Crown Court in October 2005 for stealing a credit card and fraudulently spending GBP 50,000.

row.relationships: Mathews, Peter Dennis (Associate; Enforcement)
row.profile_notes:
According to United States-Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; December 1998:
Name: James G. Oliver
Address: Grapeville, Texas
Action: Individuals Whose Registrations Were Revoked for Failure to Pay Fines, Costs And/Or Provide Proof of Restitution in Connection with Violations
Action Date: October 27, 1998

According to United States –Financial Industry Regulatory Authority; January 1997: On November 19, 1996, Peter Dennis Mathews, James Gus Oliver, Robert Alan Williky, Mark Joseph Vanyo, Lyle Emery Bettenhausen, Sr. and Gloria Ann Williams. Mathews, Oliver, Williky, Vanyo, and Bettenhausen submitted an Offer of Settlement pursuant to which Oliver was fined USD 25,000, suspended from association with any NASD member in any capacity for 90 days, and required to requalify by exam. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Mathews, Oliver, Williky, Vanyo, and Bettenhausen consented to the described sanctions and to the entry of findings that, in connection with a public offering, Mathews and Williky knowingly effected transactions that they knew or should have known, or were reckless in not knowing, were non-bona fide and designed to create the appearance of a successful completion of the offering. 

The findings also stated that Mathews and Williky knowingly or recklessly bid for and purchased, induced orders to bid for and purchase, and sold or resold, 20 percent of the offering while the distribution continued after its purported closing. Furthermore, the NASD determined that Mathews, Oliver, and Vanyo, by means of manipulative, deceptive, and other fraudulent devices and contrivances, effected a series of transactions that created actual and apparent trading in a stock, artificially supported the price, and were effected for the purpose of inducing the purchase or sale of the stock to others. The NASD found that Mathews, Oliver, and Bettenhausen made statements of material fact that they knew, had reason to know, or were reckless in not knowing, were false to induce retail customers to make investment decisions. The NASD also determined that Mathews executed transactions in the accounts of public customers that were not authorized and were made in order to support a stock price, further the aforementioned manipulative scheme, and avoid net capital deficiencies by lowering his member firm’s inventory. The findings stated that Mathews also allowed an individual, who was precluded from functioning as a registered representative, to direct trading, update quotations, direct unauthorized transactions in customer accounts, and participate in selling group and retail sales efforts at his member firm. The individual also failed to establish, maintain, and enforce supervisory procedures to assure compliance with applicable rules, misused customer funds, and engaged in private securities transactions.

According to the pina.com.fj; June 13, 2013: On June 12, 2013, Timothy Pangelinan Villagomez, former Lieutenant Governor of the Northern Mariana Islands, was resentenced to hundred and eight months imprisonment, or nine years, from the original eighty seven months for his role in the Rydlyme corruption scandal. After an 18-day trial almost four years ago, Villagomez was convicted of conspiracy to defraud the United States, wire fraud, theft concerning a program receiving federal funds, and bribery concerning a program receiving federal funds that involved the Commonwealth Utilities Corp.

According to the saipantribune.com; August 06, 2009: On August 05, 2009, Timothy Pangelinan Villagomez, former Lieutenant Governor, was sentenced to eighty seven months in prison and three years of supervised release for his role in the Rydlyme corruption scandal. Judge ordered Villagomez and the Santos couple to jointly pay USD 346,125 to the court for reimbursement to CUC. Judge also ordered Villagomez and the Santos couple to each pay a USD 400 court assessment fee and perform 200 hours of community service. Villagomez and the Santos couple were found guilty on April 24, 2009, of all charges relating to CUC's purchases of excessive amounts of a chemical, at a 400 percent markup, from companies owned by James and Joaquina Santos.

According to the saipantribune.com; August 12, 2008: On August 11, 2008, Former Lt. Gov. Timothy Villagomez entered a federal court in handcuffs to face an indictment on three felony counts of wire fraud, conspiracy and theft of federal funds, the culmination of an extensive five-month investigation by federal authorities. The indictment, charges Villagomez, Commerce Secretary James Santos, his wife Joaquina Santos-who is Villagomez's sister-and former Commonwealth Utilities Corp. executive director Anthony Guerrero with conspiring to bilk the CNMI government out of thousands of dollars through business deals involving needless chemical purchases for CUC. Villagomez and the Santos' pleaded not guilty to each of the charges against them.

According to United States - Environmental Protection Agency; March 04, 2026: On March 04, 2026, A complaint filed against Canada Holdings LLC (F/k/a Lafarge North America, Inc. and others alleging each of the defendants own or operate, owned or operated, or arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances for, at least one facility and/or vessel at the Site as defined in Section 101(9) & (28) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(9) & (28) and RCW 70A.305.020(24). 

The United States has undertaken response actions to address the release or threatened release of hazardous substances at or from the Site. In undertaking the response actions, the United States has incurred and will continue to incur response costs as defined in Section 101(25) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(25). EPA has determined that the hazardous substances at the Site present significant risks to human health and the environment, and that response actions are necessary to abate a danger or threat.

According to United States Attorney - Western District of New York; October 31, 2012: Published on that date, Lafarge North America, Inc., (LNA), a national supplier of building and construction materials and manufacturer of concrete and concrete products, has paid USD 950,000 to the United States to resolve potential civil claims by the United States under the False Claims Act. 

The matter involved highway construction projects in the Western District of New York which were funded, in part, by federal funds via the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). This required that a certain percentage of the work be performed by Disadvantaged Business Enterprises (DBE). Rayford Enterprises, Inc., d/b/a Rayford Concrete Products, a Buffalo company, was awarded subcontracts on these construction projects based on its representations that it was a DBE manufacturer of concrete. Rayford was not, in fact, a manufacturer of concrete, nor did the company have a concrete batching facility or other equipment necessary to manufacture concrete. Instead, Rayford had an agreement with Lafarge North America to manufacture and deliver concrete for these projects. Lafarge North America is not a DBE.

According to United States Department of Justice and United States Environmental Protection Agency; November 29, 2011: Published on that date, Lafarge North America Inc. agrees to pay USD 740,000 Penalty to Resolve Clean Water Act Violations in Five States. Lafarge North America Inc., one of the largest suppliers of construction materials in the United States and Canada, and four of its U.S. subsidiaries have agreed to resolve alleged Clean Water Act violations. The violations include unpermitted discharges of stormwater and failure to comply with stormwater permits at 21 stone, gravel, sand, asphalt and ready-mix concrete facilities in Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Maryland and New York.  Stormwater flowing over concrete manufacturing facilities can carry debris, sediment and pollutants including pesticides, petroleum products, chemicals and solvents, which can have a significant impact on water quality.

Lafarge will implement a nationwide evaluation and compliance program at 189 of its similar facilities in the United States to ensure they meet Clean Water Act requirements. Lafarge will also pay a penalty of USD 740,000 and implement two supplemental environmental projects, in which the company will complete conservation easements to protect approximately 166 acres in Maryland and Colorado. The value of the land has been appraised at USD 2,950,000. Lafarge will also implement one state environmentally beneficial project to support environmental training for state inspectors. The state project is valued at USD 10,000.

According to United States Environmental Protection Agency; January 21, 2010: On January 21, 2015, United States filed Clean Air Act settlement with Lafarge North America, Inc. to reduce air emissions from container glass and Portland cement plants throughout the country. The settlements covers all 13 U.S. plants owned by the Lafarge Company and two subsidiaries, the nation’s second largest manufacturer of Portland cement.

Lafarge has also agreed to pay a civil penalty of USD 5,075,000 within 30 days of entry of the consent decree. USD 3,383,000 will be paid to the United States, and the remainder will be paid to the state and local agencies participating in the settlement.

According to United States - Maryland Attorney General; May 13, 2009: Published on that date, the State of Maryland has filed suit against Lafarge North America for water pollution violations at its Texas Quarry in Cockeysville. The complaint filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County alleges 413 violations of Maryland’s water pollution laws at the concrete production and limestone quarry. Each violation carries a maximum penalty of USD 10,000.

The Texas Quarry is a surface mine operated by Lafarge and mined primarily for construction aggregate. On or about March 21, 2007, it is alleged that Lafarge discharged several tons of aggregate, crushed stone, and stone dust into nearby Goodwin Run a tributary of Gunpowder Falls and its floodplain. The amount of material discharged ranged in depth from four to 18 inches and reduced the width of the stream from approximately 15 feet wide to less than four feet wide.

According to leparisien.fr; April 28, 2026: Lafarge SA as well as its eight co-defendants appealed the decision of the Paris Court delivered on April 13, 2026. 

According to lemonde.fr; April 13, 2026: On April 13, 2026, the Criminal Court of Paris sentenced Lafarge to a EUR 1 125 000 fine for financing terrorism. The court also imposed a customs fine of EUR 4 500 000 for embargo violations to be paid jointly with other defendants. The French cement company Lafarge and its executives were found guilty of paying nearly EUR 5 600 000 to terrorist groups, including ISIS, and intermediaries in Syria between 2013 and 2014 to maintain its business operations in the area. 

According to midilibre.fr; December 19, 2025: The verdict for Lafarge SA in the financing terrorism case will be announced on April 13, 2026. 

According to lemonde.fr; December 16, 2025: On December 16, 2025, the prosecution requested a EUR 1 125 000 fine for Lafarge SA along with a partial confiscation of assets totaling EUR 30 000,000 as part of the trial for financing terrorism. Lafarge SA and four senior executives are also being prosecuted for failure to comply with international financial sanctions. In that part of the case, the prosecution has sought a joint customs fine of EUR 4 570,000.

According to actu-juridique.fr; November 18, 2025: The trial of Lafarge and its eight former executives accused of financing terrorism resumed on November 18, 2025, in Paris. It will last until December 19, 2025.

According to lefigaro.fr; November 06, 2025: The trial of Lafarge SA accused of financing terrorism was rescheduled to start on November 18, 2025.

According to lemonde.fr and lexpress.fr; October 16, 2024: On October 16, 2024, Lafarge SA and eight individuals were sent to trial for financing terrorism. In this case Lafarge is suspected of having paid EUR 5 000 000 to terrorist groups, including ISIS, and intermediaries to maintain its activities in Jalabiya between 2013 and 2014. According to the provisional calendar, the trial was scheduled to be held from November 04, 2025 till December 09, 2025.
Within another part of the case, Lafarge SA remains under investigation for crimes against humanity. 

According to lemonde.fr; February 09, 2024: On February 09, 2024, the French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office submitted a request to bring Lafarge SA and nine individuals to trial on charges of financing terrorist groups. The accusations relate to the activities of Lafarge SA in Syria in 2013-2014. Lafarge SA has already admitted paying about EUR 13 000 000 to different intermediaries in order to keep its Syrian cement factory running at that time; however, the company claimed no responsibility for the money eventually coming to the terrorist groups, allegedly including ISIS.

According to leparisien.fr; January 16, 2024: The Court of Cassation upheld the decision to place Lafarge under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity. The decision is final. The company also stays under investigation for terrorism financing allegedly committed between 2013 and 2014 in Syria. 

According to zonebourse.com; November 23, 2023: The decision of the French Cassation Court, concerning the appeal of Lafarge to drop complicity in crimes against humanity charges, has been postponed until January 16, 2024.

According to sudouest.fr; January 24, 2023: Lafarge SA has appealed before the Cassation Court the decision of the Appeal Court of Paris to place Lafarge SA under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity regarding its activities in Syria before 2014. Lafarge SA is suspected of having paid millions of dollars to jihadist groups and intermediaries to maintain its cement works in Syria between 2013 and 2014. The Cassation Court scheduled to announce its verdict on March 14, 2023.

According to United States - Department of Justice and United States Attorney - Eastern District of New York; October 18, 2022: On October 18, 2022, Lafarge S.A. and and Lafarge Cement Syria, S.A. (LCS) pleaded guilty to a one-count criminal information charging them with conspiring to provide material support and resources to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) and the al-Nusrah Front (ANF), both U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. The defendants were sentenced to three year term of probation and to pay financial penalties, including criminal fines of USD 90 780 000 and forfeiture of USD 687 000 000 totaling USD 777 780 000. The defendants’ scheme to pay ISIS and ANF in exchange for permission to operate a cement plant in Syria from August 2013 to October 2014, which enabled LCS to obtain approximately USD 70 300 000 in revenue. 

As a result of the scheme, LCS obtained approximately USD 70 300 000 in total sales revenue from August 2013 through 2014.  The gains to all participants in the conspiracy, including LCS, the intermediaries and the terrorist groups, totaled approximately USD 80 540 000.

According to france24.com; May 18, 2022: On May 18, 2022, the Appeal Court of Paris upheld the decision to place Lafarge SA under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity.

According to lefigaro.fr; March 24, 2022: On March 24, 2022, the Appeal Court of Paris heard the case of Lafarge SA regarding the complicity in crimes against humanity. The decision will be announced on May 18, 2022. In 2018, the company was formally placed under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity; however, in November 2019, the Paris Appeal Court canceled that decision. Then, in September 2021, the Cassation Court canceled the decision of the Appeal Court and sent the case back to the investigating chamber. The prosecution demands to place Lafarge SA under investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity as it, allegedly, financed via its subsidiaries the activities of ISIS.  

According to leparisien.fr; November 07, 2019: Lafarge SA is still under investigation for terrorism financing and putting the lives of others in danger in relation to its business activities in Syria. 

According to lemonde.fr and lepoint.fr; June 28, 2018: On June 28, 2018, Lafarge SA was placed under formal investigation for complicity in crimes against humanity and financing terrorist undertaking. Lafarge SA was placed under judicial supervision comprising a EUR 30 000 000 bail. Allegedly, between 2011 and 2015, Lafarge paid EUR 13 000 000 to the terrorist groups in order to maintain its business activities in Syria. 

According to leparisien.fr; June 13, 2017: On June 09, 2017, the Prosecutor's Office of Paris launched a judicial inquiry for the alleged financing of a terrorist undertaking and putting the lives of others in danger, possibly implicating LafargeHolcim. Reportedly, LafargeHolcim might have been indirectly providing funds to the armed groups in Syria. In March 2017, French company Lafarge (now renamed LafargeHolcim after a merger) admitted to indirectly financing armed groups in Syria between 2013 and 2014 in order to maintain its business activities. 

According to francais.rt.com; January 19, 2017: In September 2016, the Ministry of the Economy asked a court to investigate possible violations committed by the cement group Lafarge in Syria in relation to the prohibition to buy oil in this country enacted by the European Union in 2012. The Paris public prosecutor's office opened a preliminary investigation on these allegations in October 2016.
The French cement company is also suspected of having concluded agreements with the Islamic State. These allegations are contained in a complaint filed by NGO Sherpa in November 2016. Lafarge reportedly concluded a series of agreements with several armed groups, including the Islamic State, in order to continue its activity in northeastern Syria. These agreements allegedly reached in 2013 allowed it to continue operating its cement plant in Jalabiya before it was taken by Daesh in 2014.

According to United States - Illinois State Board of Investment; In 2018, Lafarge SA was removed from the Illinois State Board of Investment restricted list for having ties with Government of Sudan. 

According to the European Commission; March 14, 2014: In December 2010, the European Commission (EC) launched antitrust proceedings against a number of cement manufacturers for suspected breaches of EU rules banning restrictive business practices. The Commission is investigating possible import/export restrictions, market sharing and price coordination in the markets for cement, cement-based products (e.g., ready mix concrete) and other materials used to produce cement-based products (e.g., clinker, aggregates, blast-furnace slag, granulated blast-furnace slag, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, fly ash). One of the suspected companies is Lafarge.

According to United States - Illinois State Board of Investment: As of June 30, 2011 Lafarge SA was included in the prohibited list, deemed prohibited from investment for having ties with Government of Sudan. 

According to khl.com; December 10, 2010: The European Commission (EC) has launched antitrust proceedings against seven cement manufacturers active in member states. The formal proceedings were launched over suspicions that the companies acted to restrict trade flows in the European Economic Area, including organizing import and export restrictions. The alleged cartel is said to have colluded in market sharing and price fixing in the markets for cement and cement-based materials such as ready-mix concrete, clinker, aggregates, blast-furnace slag, granulated blast-furnace slag, ground granulated blast-furnace slag and fly ash. Cemex, Holcim and Heidelberg have so far confirmed that they are under investigation, while reports have cited Lafarge and Dyckerhoff as among those suspected by the EC of colluding with rivals in order to fix prices in Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK.

According to eur-lex.europa.eu; June 17, 2010: On June 17, 2010, the European Union's highest court has upheld a EUR 249,600,000 penalty imposed on Lafarge SA by the European Commission in November 2002. The European Court of Justice dismissed Lafarge’s appeal for an annulment of a reduction of its fine in its entirety.

According to the European Commission; July 08, 2008: The Court of First Instance confirmed the existence and duration of the cartel and upheld the fines imposed on all but one addressee (BPB PLC). On November 27, 2002, the Commission fined BPB PLC (United Kingdom), Gebrüder Knauf Westdeutsche Gipswerke KG (Germany), Société Lafarge SA (France) and Gyproc Benelux SA/NV (Belgium) for participating in a cartel on the market for plasterboard, a product which is widely used in the building industry and by DIY practitioners, in the United Kingdom, Germany, France and the Benelux countries between 1992 and 1998.

According to aachener-zeitung.de; February 18, 2007: Six cement makers face a court ruling in Germany on whether a group of customers can claim damages to the tune of EUR 100 000 000 (USD 133 000 000) if the companies are found guilty of price fixing. The claims stem from an investigation and subsequent fines handed to the cement makers by the country’s Federal Cartel Office in 2003 after it uncovered evidence of price fixing. The companies involved in the case are Dyckerhoff AG, HeidelbergCement AG, Holcim Ltd of Switzerland and Schwenk Zement KG of Germany as well as Lafarge SA of France and Ireland’s Readymix Plc, now owned by Cemex SA.

According to Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa; February 23, 2004: In February 2004, the Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa annulled the tender offers for the exchange of Lafarge bonds. It had previously suspended the offer, which had been made in Italy via the a central securities depository for 90 days as a precautionary measure. 

According to Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa; November 24, 2003: In November 2003, the Italian Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa ordered the preventive suspension for 90 days of the exchange offer for Lafarge bonds. The orders are based on the fact that the Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa has no record of having received either notice of such a public offer or the information document to be published, as required by the Italian law.

According to European Commission; November 27, 2002: The European Commission imposed fines totaling EUR 478 000 000 on four companies which operated a long-running cartel on the market for plasterboard, a product which is widely used in the building industry and by DIY practitioners. The cartel affected 80% of consumers in the European Union, namely in France, the United Kingdom, Germany and the Benelux countries. Two of the companies involved, Lafarge and BPB, were committing their second infringement of EU law on restrictive agreements, having already been fined once in 1994. The Commission has consequently decided to impose the fines totaling EUR 249 600,000 on Lafarge SA.

According to curia.europa.eu; March 15, 2000: Lafarge Coppée SA had its fine reduced from EUR 23 900 000 to EUR 14 248 000 by the judgment of the Court of First Instance.

According to European Commission; November 30, 1994: The European Commission decided to impose fines on the European Cement Association (Cembureau), eight national cement associations and 33 European cement producers for infringements of Article 85 of the EC Treaty involving their participation from 1983 in a general market-sharing agreement, transnational restrictive practices and restrictive practices relating to exports (market sharing and exchanges of information). The firms concerned are based in all the Member States and in some of the EFTA  countries  (Norway, Sweden and Switzerland).
Lafarge Coppée S.A. was imposed fines totaling EUR 23 900 000.

Description:
Lafarge SA, a French cement company, merged with Swiss company Holcim to create LafargeHolcim in July 2015. Lafarge SA continued its activity as a wholly-owned subsidiary of LafargeHolcim.

row.details: enforcement: Environmental Crimes | US-U.S. Environmental Protection Agency | United States; adverse_media: Pollution | Incident
row.relationships: Canada Holdings LLC (AffiliatedCompany; Enforcement); Lafarge Midwest, Inc (AffiliatedCompany; AdverseMedia,Enforcement)
row.profile_notes:
According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; January 21, 2010: The United States today filed two major Clean Air Act settlements to reduce air emissions from container glass and Portland cement plants throughout the country, announced Cynthia Giles, assistant administrator for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Enforcement and Compliance Assurance and Ignacia S. Moreno, Assistant Attorney General for the Environment and Natural Resources Division. The settlements cover 15 U.S. plants owned by Saint-Gobain Containers, Inc., the nation’s second largest container glass manufacturer, and all 13 U.S. plants owned by the Lafarge Company and two subsidiaries, the nation’s second largest manufacturer of Portland cement. These settlements are the first system-wide settlements for these sectors under the Clean Air Act and require pollution control upgrades, acceptance of enforceable emission limits and payment of civil penalties.

Lafarge has also agreed to pay a civil penalty of USD 5,075,000 within 30 days of entry of the consent decree. USD 3,383,000 will be paid to the United States, and the remainder will be paid to the state and local agencies participating in the settlement.

row.profile_notes:
According to the Punjab Police (Pakistan); May 07, 2024: In May 2024, the Organized Crime Unit (OCU) of Lahore police has busted an international gang, including four members of the same family, that was supplying narcotics and party drugs to the upper-class youth. The ‘Jordan Gang,’ including four members of the same family, was operating from Central Asia, Mexico, Canada, USA and some other countries and supplying highly expensive drugs in Lahore and Multan. Efforts of police culminated in a coordinated overnight raid on three locations in Phase VI of the DHA, resulting in the arrest of key members of the gang including Muhammad Ali, Uzair, Muhammad Nadeem, Samina Iftikhar and Fatima Zahra. However, Ayub Jordan is still at large as he is operating from Thailand. After an extensive two-month intelligence gathering and covert operation, the unit busted the gang. He said the elusive gang leader, Ayub Khan alias Jordan, was operating secretly and nobody knew his true identity. The OCU managed to infiltrate Jordan’s network through a plan. Multiple purchases were made to gain the trust of Jordan’s associates, leading to crucial breakthroughs in investigation.

Deals were offered to students and other citizens through fake IDs on social media and the gang was operating many bank accounts in the name of a woman suspect, Samina Iftikhar, and her son Uzair to obtain money. Ayub alias Jordan and Muhammad Ali are her two other sons. Ayub Khan alis Jordan was living in Thailand along with his other family members and Muhammad Ali and Uzair were his brothers. Jordan was operating the network for the last 12 years to smuggle drugs into Pakistan from Canada, the USA and Mexico. Investigation revealed that the gang had purchased three villas in the DHA with money generated through drug trafficking. The family was allegedly using these villas to store and supply drugs in the provincial capital and other cities. row.profile_notes:
According to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) - Govt. of Pakistan; June 2014: Anti Terrorism Act 1997 inspite of various shortcomings has provided effective mechanism to police stations to conduct surveillance of activists on Schedule-IV of the Act in order to curb and prevent acts of terrorism by members of proscribed organizations. Section-11EE prescribes restrictions on movements, residence & visits of these suspects. Section 11EE also states that suspects before leaving the area of residence have to seek prior permission of Officer In charge of Police Station. Their assets & sources of incomes will also be subject to investigation. ATA-1997 further provides that any person who violates any direction or order shall be punishable with an imprisonment of up to 3 years or fine or both. However, these provisions of ATA 1997 are not enforced effectively or uniformly. It is very rare to observe registration of cases against suspects u/s 11EE ATA 1997. CTW FIA has prepared the consolidated list of Activists on basis of data provided by CTD/CIDs and Home Departments.

Once all provinces have updated lists of Activists on Schedule-IV the Federal & Provincial Govts. may also consider some amendments in ATA in order to deny or restrict issuance of passports, arms licence, driving licence, credit card, internet usage etc to these suspects so that they cannot easily travel, associate, rent building, buy weapons/transport/ dual use chemicals, harbor terrorists, use internet etc, and conduct terrorist attacks freely.

row.relationships: Dash, Rajesh (Associate; AdverseMedia); Tripathy, Biju (Associate; AdverseMedia); Dash, Prasanjit (Associate; AdverseMedia); Mantri, Mukesh (Associate; AdverseMedia); Samantara, Pradeep Kumar (Associate; AdverseMedia)
row.profile_notes: According to the odishabytes.com; December 23, 2023: In December 2023, Abdul Rahman was arrested along with other associates in connection with a credit card fraud amounting to INR 80,000,000. The complainant alleged that a credit card was issued in his name without his knowledge, and he was denied loan over poor CIBIL score because of the transactions made using it. The outstanding dues of the credit card was INR 140,000. During investigation identified Biju Tripathy as the person using the credit card. During the raid on his house, 450 credit and debit cards, INR 700,000 cash, 50 cheque books, 78 passbooks, 3 sacks of money receipt, six swipe machines and as many mobile phones were seized. Prasanjit Dash used to collect personal credentials of different persons to apply for credit cards and also fraudulently received those cards and used it. Simultaneously Pradeep Kumar Samantara, who was the employee of a bank, used to issue those cards in the name of Rakesh Kumar with forged documents. Mukesh Mantri introduced Prasanjit Dash with Biju Tripathy, who used to collect cash by using the credit card at POS counters like hospitals and OMFED booths in connivance with billing agents. Abdul Rahman and Rajesh Dash are hospital employees who worked as billing agents. Biju Tripathy used pay some commission to the billing agents and invest the remaining cash to earn profits. Police have calculated INR 20,000,000 of the money receipt seized.

row.details: enforcement: Terrorism | PK-Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) - Govt. of Pakistan | Pakistan
row.profile_notes:
According to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) - Govt. of Pakistan; June 2014: Anti Terrorism Act 1997 inspite of various shortcomings has provided effective mechanism to police stations to conduct surveillance of activists on Schedule-IV of the Act in order to curb and prevent acts of terrorism by members of proscribed organizations. Section-11EE prescribes restrictions on movements, residence & visits of these suspects. Section 11EE also states that suspects before leaving the area of residence have to seek prior permission of Officer Incharge of Police Station. Their assets & sources of incomes will also be subject to investigation. ATA-1997 further provides that any person who violates any direction or order shall be punishable with an imprisonment of up to 3 years or fine or both. However, these provisions of ATA 1997 are not enforced effectively or uniformly. It is very rare to observe registration of cases against suspects u/s 11EE ATA 1997. CTW FIA has prepared the consolidated list of Activists on basis of data provided by CTD/CIDs and Home Departments.

Once all provinces have updated lists of Activists on Schedule-IV the Federal & Provincial Govts. may also consider some amendments in ATA in order to deny or restrict issuance of passports, arms licence, driving licence, credit card, internet usage etc to these suspects so that they cannot easily travel, associate, rent building, buy weapons/transport/ dual use chemicals, harborterrorists, use internet etc, and conduct terrorist attacks freely.

One of the suspects listed by District Quetta is: Abdul Rahman

Father's Name: Abdul Aziz cast Syed 
Address/Police Station: Kuchlak Bazar Quetta
Position: Terrorist
Party Affiliation: Terrorist
Remarks: Personal file not yet be opened by local Police, no monitoring reported.
